review_text: I read this book in two days, on the way to and from An Evening With Neil Gaiman. It is the perfect book. If you removed two adult scenes it could be enjoyed by all ages. Those two scenes are important though and I am glad he geared this read to an adult audience. It has all the magic and fantasy I've come to expect from Neil Gaiman.

SUPER CUTE! 
 *Warning: This review contains spoilers from Flat-Out Love, and should not be read without reading the previous book.* 
 Flat-Out Celeste follows Matt's younger sister, Celeste (If you haven't already guessed from the title) on an adventure of finding her own love. Celeste is now a senior in high school and isn't completely social. She's very independent and she speaks crisply and formally. As the year passes by, she learns more about who she wants to be and where she wants to go in life through her coming-to-be college preview. In her expedition to find where she wants to go in life, she makes new friends and she learns that she's not useless to others. She's going to make a big difference on some people's lives. 
 Colleges WANT Celeste. She's applying for all the Ivy Leagues,  and she makes them, considering what awesome intellectual smartness she has, it's not that surprising , but Matt also wants her to branch out and try something new. She soon receives and email from Justin, a student rep for Barton College in San Diego. What starts as a chain of emails and soon text messages, leads to real life, and learning what one really wants to be and who she wants in her life, teaching her about love and acceptance. 
 The Awesome: 
 -Justin was totally an awesome guy. He didn't judge Celeste, and he had his own set of quirks that he wasn't that embarrassed by. 
 -The characters really mature. Celeste learned what she wanted and she really worked towards an awesome future. 
 -The secondary characters were also quite supportive. Celeste really made friends are branched out socially. 
 -Celeste took risks. Some characters weep and get all depressed, but Celeste knew what she wanted and she worked towards it. 
 -The writing made everything sound stunning. The descriptions were beautiful. 
 -It wasn't just about Celeste. This story worked to focus on a lot of characters and their relationships. Justin was focused on quite a bit, but so were the secondary characters like Dallas. 
 -More than one love story :)  There was also focus on Matt, which I thought was awesome since he was the focus of the previous book. Matt was an awesome brother. Matt and Julie broke up, and as they struggle in their break up, their relationship was truly amazing by the end.  
 -The comedy. And Matt's T-Shirts! 
 The only thing that wasn't PERFECT and kind of annoyed me, was that Celeste didn't completely tell Justin about Flat Finn and that her speech was so formal. But that's not that big of a deal. 
 Overall: If you've read Flat-Out Love, read this NOW. It's awesome!

It is so nice to occasionally venture into another genre. I think it gives that book an unfair advantage because it's much harder to give an objective review of a genre that you don't normally read. You are either unfairly critical because obviously you generally avoid that genre and it turns out you had reason to all along. Or you are like me and like the change of pace so much, that it doesn't matter if it's not all that good (this definitely doesn't pertain to the romance genre however, still don't like that). So, that really long introduction is basically me saying, I would have given this book less stars if it weren't for the fact that it's the first horror book I've read in a very long time. 
 It was nice to read a book that was a little more intense and gave you tangible, physical reasons to keep reading. It was very obvious that something would be happening to them (either dying or getting rescued or saving themselves), so I just had to keep reading to find out what. The premise of the story was good, and I liked the small details that were revealed along the way. And I like that not all questions were answered because let's face it, that's how life is. 
 The problem is that I kind of already knew what would happen. From the time they were on the hill, I felt like I could see the rest of the story fold out and when I finished, it was kind of like, "Huh, yeah, I'm not surprised." Nothing shocked or scared me, as I think it should have. I wanted it to scare me, but I just didn't really care about the characters enough to be scared for their sake. 
 That leads me to one of my other issues with this book. The characters were just not that interesting. He tried a few times, but really, I still didn't care about them at all. I can't decide if it was clever or stupid of him to basically draw attention to the fact that his characters fit into simple horror story molds halfway through the book. It still didn't really work out for me though.

I loved this book! :) 
 It was such a lovely surprise! 
 I adored the hero, Alexander! He's stuttering and having enormous problems because of that. He's a laird and should be a strong, determined leader, but with he's having problems speaking, so it' very difficult for him! 
 Still he's such a dear, honorable man that you cannot avoid suffering for him when he's struggling with words. And it happens in the most unconvenient moments: when he's excited or when he's angry, or stressed about something. 
 Hannah was also a very interesting heroine. She's strong willed, but at the same time very compassionate and sweet in her own way. 
 I loved how their story progressed: slowly and sweetly. 
 Hannah at first doesn't know what to think about her brand new husband: he isn't talking to her! But he's passionate and very skilled in other departments! LOL 
 Alexandred has fallen in love with his brand new wife, but has enormous trouble telling her that - obviously! So he's showing her in other ways! *wink, wink* 
 A very enjoyable and very well written! Recommanded!

The political aspects of Rand's work are interesting, and I was able to somewhat enjoy the story on that merit. Unfortunately, it is not just a political picture of what happens in extreme socialism/communism. The characters are boring, the morality is awful, and as a story it kind of flops. When the only way to get your point across is to write a 40 page dialogue-dump by using a character as a mouthpiece, you know you're doing something wrong. The story is interesting for its political outlook, but only for that.

The 2nd book in the Fallen series. This book is probably my most favourite on out the series (though I haven't read Rapture yet). 
 Characters 
 The characters in this book were the same as the characters in the first book, with a few additions. 
 I think Luce and Daniel weren't as "bonded" in this book as they are in the other books. Personally, I think that it made the story more interesting to see how they responded to that. 
 Luce is very hard to understand and her character is very mysterious even though the story is being told from her point of view. She was definitely stronger in this book than she was in the first book. I think that she still had the same worries and weakness, but she has learnt how to fade them out a little. 
 Daniel, who we don't hear much of in this book until the end, hasn't changed much, but his love for Luce is more defined in his actions. 
 Plot 
 The plot for Torment was more interesting than the plot for Fallen, plainly because there were more things going on at once, and it was more fast paced with higher points of climax and tension. 
 The ending for this book was a great way to open up new problem for the third book : Passion

I really enjoyed this book!!! Yay, I've always liked Becca Fitzpatrick's writing and looking at the reviews I didn't want to think that this book was being put down because of people's distaste to the Hush Hush series, but personally I enjoyed it. 
 "You never know what you're going to have to face, so you'd better be prepared." 
 Britt Pfeiffer has always been safe in her life. Going on this trip though will prove that she's willing to be adventurous, especially to her ex-boyfriend who will meet them at their cabin since he is her best friend's brother. 
 Heading up the mountains, Britt and her best friend get caught up in a drastic storm that leads them to unexpected danger. Stuck in the snow storm with no communication, the gas wouldn't last in the car to keep them warm for very long. They needed to find somewhere else. And when they think they've found their greatest chance of surviving, things don't look too good for them. Their lives are suddenly in danger in the presence of the two men who take them in and there is no where to go. 
 "Because those four days in the mountains, they changed us." 
 Seeing Mason again after their brief encounter at the store the day before startles her. But even though Mason is a part of what's going on, Britt gets the feeling that she can get through to him to help. And when things go horribly wrong, she realises she actually needs him to survive the storm up in the catastrophic mountain more than she wishes. 
 Until she figures out who he really is. 
 "If I had known things would turn out this way, I would have trained harder. I would have learned to take care of myself." 
 In this book, yes there was a bit of romance, but it definitely didn't consume the story which was more about survival. It more endeared it and it added a really nice touch to the scary situation that the girls were in and I loved how it played out. 
 I really liked Britt's character, yes, she could be gullible and naive but at times she was able to think straight and help herself. Not all characters are perfect and even though we may take them as annoying and throw the book across the room in frustration, I didn't get this feeling with Britt even though her thinking could be disliked. She had her moments and I still enjoyed reading this book which I can happily say with 4 stars. 
 It was a book on survival. And the truth behind people. Who you trust and who you shouldn't. Even if you thought you knew who they were. 
 And how wrong you can be. 
 But of course that goes both ways. 
 "More tongue exercises? Would have thought you'd had enough last night." 
 "Go to hell." 
 "Sorry, love, but we're already there." 
 Even in Hush Hush, I loved Fitzpatrick's witty comebacks that she gets into the story and I found more in this book too which I loved. Just added a touch of sassiness to the book. 
 "I can't let go of you, Britt. And I don't want you to let go of me." 
 I really enjoyed this book and I'm delighted I did. I love Becca Fitzpatrick's writing. The story was well balanced and the characters were good too. Britt's experience didn't pass without teaching her a few things about life so I found there was definitely character development. It was a different story for a change so I'm glad to have read it.

Gin Blanco did not initially strike me as particularly impressive, and her attempts to defend herself and her line of work by pretending she was probably more upright than all the corrupt masqueraders around her didn't work. But as the plot progresses, you discover that that there's much to enjoy about Gin: her sharp wit, her astute analysis, her easy affection for Finn and all the people she loves, her disgust for injustice. 
 Gin's associates were equally fun to read about, and I especially liked the funny and sweet Finnegan Lane. His appearances added comic relief and enhanced the storyline. 
 Donovan Caine, however, has got to be one of the dumbest detectives I have come across; I mean, seriously?! In his haste to pass judgment and voice disgust at every turn, he misses the most obvious things. Doofus. 
 The plot was well done; long, though. But I read for the characters. Here's looking forward to more adventures with Gin and her crew. I hope said adventures are faster paced, though :-)

I read this on my way to Amsterdam on Wednesday; on the train and then the plane, and finished it that night in my hotel room in Den Haag. And I did make some notes for my review but now I can't think of anything more specific... I think I was close to giving this five stars. The writing was lovely and the story intriguing but overall, it's not quite a five-star book. 
 I liked how Winifred's own story began to unravel through her writing of Wendy's. At first what she's writing is portrayed as just fiction, then possibly wishful fiction, then you find out that it's actually true - her own story that she can't get away from. The scene at the Romanian orphanage was just terrible, that's THE moment when it really hits you how the fiction is reality.  It was a bit low of... what was his name again? One of the gay boys... a bit low of him to 'out' Winnie as he did, but I liked how he kept in contact with her after that. I can imagine them being good friends in the future. 
 Winifred isn't all that likeable of a character, until you start to learn more about her. Then she at least becomes more sympathetic and interesting. Allegra I did not like - I was biased against her due to her name and then she wasn't wildly likeable in any case. 
 I LOVED all the references to other British books thrown in, especially all the childrens' stories. The line about Muggles and Mennyms and daemons made me happy :D And I was really interested to learn that the name Wendy wasn't even really a name until J.M. Barrie came along! I loved also the use of one of my favourite songs, Not a Day Goes By. And was it just me or where there really a lot of vague references to Maguire's other books?! The phrase What-the-Dickens popped up, as well as a few Ozian mentions... I just found that fun :) 
 The incident with the nails pulling themselves back into the wall creeped me the hell out btw. And Mrs. Maddingly and the cats grossed me out, too much :( I kind of found the whole Gervasa-possessing-Winifred story a bit too weird for me, though it was funny at times. 
 My favourite quote, which I had to write down, has to be "So it was only in Paris, apparently, near the train station that brought visitors from England, that the French behaved as if they'd never come across the English language before." The scene in the restaurant was rather priceless XD 
 I also loved reading Wilhelm Muller's Erstarrung (from the Winterreise CD which Winifred was playing), not least because I could actually understand it all before I read the translation. 
 Ich such im Schnee vergebens 
 Nach ihrer Tritte Spur, 
 Wo sie an meinem Arme 
 Durchstrich die grune Flur. 
 Ich will den Boden kussen, 
 Durchdringen Eis und Schnee 
 Mit meinen heissen Tranen 
 Bis ich die Erde, die Erde seh.

This book is the second in a series. If you've not read the first book, be sure to do so before you start this one. This book picks up right where the last book left off and hardly looks back. It has been several months since I read Mrs. Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children, but it didn't take long for me to remember the previous story. 
 The series is made unique by the photographs that dot the pages. The author has put effort into finding unique photographs from generations ago. The pictures fit so effortlessly into the story that a reader may assume the pictures were posed just for the sake of what is written. However, the author just does a peculiarly great job of weaving the story and the photographs together. 
 Keep in mind that this is a young adult book written about children (with unusual talents). But it's also much more. There is adventure and danger in these pages. The story continues moving throughout the book and should be enjoyable to anyone wanting to read about a fantasy world. It took Ransom Riggs two and a half years to write this book, but I am anxiously awaiting the publication of the third book.

I liked this book for a variety of reasons, but it has a fatal flaw. Georgina's dream imprisonment feels both like a writer's convenience and like Mead wrote herself into a corner. I have no idea how Mead managed do that. Georgina observing the other characters and coming to conclusions/realizations feels a little like lazy writing, but Mead doesn't really leave herself another option as she sticks her main character in a dream state for a chunk of the book.  Seeing bits of Georgina's past was neat, but there wasn't enough of it and it was punctuated with too many introspective moments.

So with the release of the new Pirates movie this year.. I wanted a little Pirate fever to stir.. and it did .. I loved this book!!! 
 Okay, before I just explode from fangirling.. I'll explain about what the book is about.. 
 Princess Alosa is the Daughter of the self titled Pirate King Kalligan. He has sent her on a mission to to find one of three maps that show the location of Isla de Canta. A Island full of untold riches and treasure. The Pirate King wants the treasure to ensure he stays King for a very long time.. 
 Alosa is 'kidnapped' by the captain of the Night Farer Ship, looking for a ransom from her father. Alosa is on a mission to find map.. but the intriguing first Mate -The captain's Brother- is a little too tempting.. 
 This is a debut book for Tricia Levenseller, but it doesn't show. She made me completely envious of the world they lived in, even with the violence and thievery. Her descriptions of the sea and the world were vivid. 
 "I live on the cusp of two worlds, trying desperately to fit into one." 
 I loved Alosa. She was strong, and enough of a Pirate to know she wasn't a pretender ( I hate those) She had enough fierceness without being a bitch, and I loved it. 
 She had some of that bizarre eccentricities that Jack Sparrow had that I love for example: 
 "If you're sorry, that means you want forgiveness. Is that what you're asking for? If you want forgiveness, that means you want to make things right. And if you want to make things right, that means that you don't intend to put me in harm's way again. So, if you are saying you're sorry, I don't think you understand what that entails." 
 Riden's allegiance to his nauseous inducing brother was commendable. Even, when he did not agree with his brother's actions he remained faithful. 
 The Romance between the two was even paced, steady and a bit slow, but it was clear the feelings were manifesting over the course of the book. Alosa & Riden were cut from the cloth, but there is much more that can be developed between the characters. 
 I checked out Tricia Levenseller GoodReads page which says that the series is a duology, and the final book is out in February 2018. Definitely, pre-order!!!

 Okaaay... so. This book. Now that I look at it now, I feel really disappointed. I thought that so much was going to happen, and it could have. Overall, this book was a let down, but good nonetheless.

 2) The switching off between Hana and Lena's POV. I thought it was really interesting since we haven't heard from Hana in awhile. It was especially interesting once we got to the ending, where their two stories collide. 
 3) GRACE SURVIVING.  That is all. 
 4) Seeing more of, as we all expected, Lena's mom. 
 And.. I don't really know. This ending leaves me quite iffy. Its not as solid as I hoped it would be. Meh.

 I think I may have read this book wrong. I loved it, yet it is #1 on the GoodReads list of of "Worst Stephen King" books, which I truly cannot understand. One, "Cell" is obviously his worst book, and two, "Gerald's Game" is a horrifying psychological novel about a woman who survives and lives to tell her story- and she is NOT lying. 
 Jessie Burlingame is 39 and married to Gerald, an overweight borderline-alcoholic lawyer who is looking to spice things up in the bedroom. They take an off-season retreat to their summer home where Gerald handcuffs Jessie's wrists to the headboard and intends to have his wicked way with her. Only Jessie changes her mind before they can begin, causing a row between the couple that leaves Gerald dead on the floor of a heart attack and Jessie still chained to the bed. 
 This situation would be horrifying enough on its own- being completely stuck in an abandoned home, unable to break free or call for help. But soon, Jessie begins to hear conflicting voices telling her what to do- the bold, honest one is Ruth, her college friend whom she later records this story for, and Jessie's alter-ego, the mild "Goodwife" Burlingame. Jessie alternately takes comfort in these voices and shuns them until she realizes they are trying to get her to recall her repressed memories of childhood sexual abuse because it will reveal a way to break loose from the handcuffs. 
 And to top it off, someone is there in the room with her at night. We don't think he's real, sometimes Jessie doesn't think he's real, but by God, he's real. 
 This was a page-turner from start to finish. Jessie was an interesting and reliable narrator who had a real story to tell, and the recollection of her sexual abuse at the hands of her father during the solar eclipse in 1963 was painful to read, but King handled it with grace and understanding. We were always on Jessie's side- we never doubted her pain, anguish, and torture, and we felt every cramp and every jolt of terror as she lay handcuffed in that room. I was absolutely terrified during the last 50 pages because I thought for sure King was going to make Jessie a madwoman who saw shadows that gave her the creeps. But no, everything that happened to Jessie was real- from the dog eating her husband to the wicker basket of bones and jewels. 
 This book may have been a little scattered, but I think it came together in the end. It did have a lot going on- Jessie's ordeal was enough, and then adding a necrophiliac serial killer just seems unfair!- but like I said, I think it all worked out. I will always be confused as to why people seem to hate this book so much, but I guess it all depends on taste. 
 **SPOILERS END*** 
 If you do plan to read this, go into it without knowing anything about the book. It could have ended any way, and it is best to be surprised.

This book was very good. It blends real life history and people with a fictional case and is done so well you can almost believe that it really happened. The author did his research on the ear, the people and the places for this story and it shows. It flowed very smoothly and wasn't slow at all but didn't rush at break neck speed to a conclusion either. You got to figure out the mystery at the pace of the characters, there was no give away or obvious clues here. It was very detailed without bogging the reader down and that was great, you could imagine being there with these characters. It is a bit of a dark story so those with trigger to violence and can't handle gore should be aware. However it's all correct for the time period, it's not over done it's just what you would have seen or heard at that time. Very realistic to life and an interesting read.

Ok, I have a confession to make: 
 I was a Jojo snob, I thought she wrote same-old-same-old run-of-the-mill romances for middle aged ladies. In fact, I presented one her books (not this one) to my mom, who's middle aged and loves romances, last year. She loved it! 
 I owe Jojo an apology! From one Jojo to another, you lady are a great story teller! I wasn't put off by one single second in this book. It made me cry and smile and root for it's characters. 
 Not saying much for fear of spoiling people but I do think this one deserves a sequel, yes? YES?

Oh boy I didn't know I was in for a treat, What a wonderful read that was, I'm not one to give 5 stars lightly but I loved this book SO much. The plot grabbed my attention but once I begun reading, it completely sucked me in, I loved the slow building tension between the characters, their chemistry, the dialogue, everything was just perfect . To sum up the plot, Kate Donovan is a 31 year old social worker, who takes some time off from her job to accompany her grandmother to her hometown and help her with the restoration of her childhood home, the man in charge of the job is Matt Jarreau, an ex-hockey player who gave up his job to live a reclusive live, away from family and friends, after the tragic death of his first wife. Kate insists on befriending Matt after realizing there's some deep sadness in him, Matt rejects her attempt to form a friendship and always turns down her dinner invitations, he is still grieving his wife's death and does not want to become attached to anyone, at first Kate's proximity scares him, he does not want to feel anything as it makes him feel vulnerable and he's afraid of pursuing a relationship with her, but Kate is a determined character, and I loved that about her. If you like christian fiction, I'd recommend it, if you don't like it I'd recommend it too, as it is not "preachy" I think it would appeal to everybody who enjoys a nice romance novel.

At first I didn't think I was going to like this book. The first few chapters, before the author actually arrives in prison, present a rushed backstory and are not that interesting. I think the memoir would have been better if it had begun in medias res, with flashbacks as needed. I say this because the bulk of the book, set at a women's federal prison in Danbury, Connecticut, is excellent. Piper Kerman writes with a unique voice and really gives a sense of prison life and of all the problems with our prison system through the stories of her and her fellow inmates; she rarely preaches. 
 Kerman is obviously from a different background than most prisoners: she is rich and white. Her elite educational background is no doubt a major factor in her being able to produce the book's excellent prose. We come so close to the prisoners who are truly trapped in the vicious cycle of incarceration in America that we wish, someday, for a book written by the likes of Pop or Delicious.

Oh my god, Lex doesn't disappoint! Shameless is a bit darker than her Dearest series but her writing is still flawless and it doesn't change a thing for me. I have to point out that I live in Boston (which is why I wish Brady was real so I could kidnap him ;) ) but I felt like I joined Brady on his journey to Texas and was there to witness every moment with Izzy and Kat. Lex Martin creates pure magic. <3 
 After a tragic accident involving Brady's brother, he leaves Boston and heads to Texas to take care of what needs to be done in times like these. What he doesn't expect is Katherine, Izzy, the farm, and all the responsibilities that must be taken care of. Dealing with his own financial problems and the health of his father back home leaves Brady struggling with decisions. And as he spends more time with Kat, his decisions get even harder. He had a plan: Take care of everything then head back to Boston with his niece. But sometimes plans change. And they're life-altering. 
 Katherine is a godsend. Without her, Brady would be lost. She's so smart and amazing and resilient but she doesn't want to take credit for all she has done and that makes me love her even more. Witnessing her grow as a character was phenomenal. I love shy heroines that know what they want. Add the fact that she's Spanish and my girl gets even more points! Katherine's back story and everything she had to deal with broke my heart but seeing her as the woman she is now, put it back together. I feel like so many people can relate to Kat. Even if it's a tiny part, you should be proud of you who are and where your family comes from. Never let anyone take that away from you! 
 And Izzy, oh that sweet, sweet girl is so precious and so damn cute! I admit, reading about Brady and his moments with Izzy made my ovaries explode. I mean, come on, this big tatted guy getting all cute with a one-year-old is a sight to see and swoon over. *heart eyes* Plus, Brady with Bandit the raccoon, yeah, I can read this book forever and fall in love with it over and over again. 
 Shameless is not an ugly cry kind of book but it will hit you with all the feels. To me, it's all I need. :)

This was a tepid fantasy playing to many of the classic fantasy tropes. The characters were interesting, but also in a tepid way. The author's heavy use of passive voice and omniscient third person perspective puts a lot of distance between the characters and the reader so that I never felt fully engaged. This was a quick, good story but not one I'd be tempted to pick up again. I liked the heroine's self-reliance and the fact she didn't have to fall in love with the first guy that came along. I probably won't read the rest in the series.

3.5 stars, really. 
 My issue with this book lies solely with St Vincent and how he ended up "kidnapping" Lillian. I just...basically from the time he's introduced, I thought he would be the perfect opposite for Evie. And I could just SEE it.  Not knowing at the time that they would actually *be* paired off, of course.  So I was annoyed by the unnecessary drama of this plot twist. 
 Actually, the high drama was something that had already bothered me slightly at the end of the first book, but less so than it did here. I liked the first half of this a lot, but then it started going downhill just a little bit.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Adrienne agrees to watch her friend's inn over a long off-season weekend with just one guest on the books. It's the perfect chance to escape her messy and frustrating life. What she doesn't know is that this guest is doing the same and they will help each other move on... 
 The last time I read Nicholas Sparks was in high school and I loved him. I wanted to read everything by him. Maybe I've changed too much or maybe it's just the fault of this single novel but I didn't get swept away like I had before. It was too unbelievable. I mean, they are declaring neverending true love for each other after one day. It just doesn't work like that. I didn't particularly care for either of them so that didn't help me buy into the romance. I'll probably give Sparks another shot at some point, but not anytime soon.

 The Actor and the Housewife was an emotional journey full of Shannon's usual charm and wit. It explored really well the idea of whether a men and a women can be "just friends." This was so different than any other shifter story that I've read so far that I'm standing here completely baffled. Everything in this story impressed me, from the quality of writing to the incredibly well-realised characters. Also, despite being very fast paced, Strength of the Pack didn't feel rushed. The author developed the story in a manner that allowed for the characters to establish the relationships going on between them and for us readers to get used to them and to the slightly different world created for this story to unfold in. 
 Regarding Lucas and Noah, I absolutely loved both of them as individuals and as a couple, even though I couldn't relate to any of them at all, since they are both super alpha soldiers and I'm way far from being anything even resembling that. At first I wasn't buying the way the two of them got close to each other and started having a relationship, but then, as the author further explained the culture of the werewolves I got how things worked and the relationship between Lucas and Noah became much more believable and enjoyable to read. 
 The relationship between the main characters and how it was slowly developed was quite different from other shifter stories that I've read to this point. It was so much more raw, emotional and intense that, at times, I found myself breathless. There wasn't insta anything, though. Everything going on was explained in detail by the author and, surprisingly enough, it all made sense - when you put into consideration all the new lore and the fresh take on the mechanics of werewolves-humans relationships explored here, of course. 
 What I found most interesting was that it seemed like McKenna really made an effort to put emotion in every little scene possible between the main characters. She did an awesome job of exposing raw reactions that real wolves would have to all the werewolf characters, specially to Noah. The use of such writing device made all the sex scenes - and there are many - feel way hotter than I was expecting they would be. I could feel the emotions emanating from the pages at all times and it was very satisfying to read. 
 In addition, I loved how Noah and Lucas weren't kept apart for long periods of time, as it's usually the case when it comes to stories dealing with the military scene. God knows how I dread reading this kinds of stories, since I know that, all of a sudden, one of the main characters might be dragged to an entirely different place than the other main character is and then all the romance usually becomes a big ball of angst and the story itself invariably tends to become dull and uninteresting to me. It was not the case here, fortunately. Of course, a big chunk of page time was spent in missions and fights and all that comes with military stories, but Lucas and Noah were always together, so I didn't mind it at all. 
 If there's one thing to complain, one thing that didn't make sense to me, it would be the naivety and uncharacteristic innocence - to put it lightly - coming from Lucas regarding his understanding of the true nature of his relationship with Noah. It was clear for all those willing to see that Noah was deeply in love with him from the very beginning of their relationship. However, for some reason which still escapes my understanding, it took lots and lots of time for Lucas to finally get his head out of his ass and understand that what was going on between them was love, not lust caused by werewolves' rituals. It just pissed me off. Also, the epilogue was horrible. I was expecting to see at least a little bit of Lucas and Noah just interacting as a couple without any of the military bullshit going on around them, but I guess the author felt too lazy to write one chapter about that. 
 That said, Strength of the Pack is still an incredible high-quality story that I would totally recommend for anyone to read. I'm not sure if I'm going to keep reading this series, since I saw the next instalments are not about Lucas and Noah, so I'm afraid the next books will be just mere slightly different copies of this one; just more of the same, only with lesser quality. So I guess I'll be stopping reading this series here, but I am extremely curious to read more works from this author. 
 Anyway, that's it for this one. Ciao!

***Review posted on The Eater of Books! blog*** 
 Pointe by Brandy Colbert 
 Publisher: Penguin 
 Publication Date: April 10, 2014 
 Rating: 4 stars 
 Source: ARC (traded) 
 Summary (from Goodreads): 
 Theo is better now. 
 She's eating again, dating guys who are almost appropriate, and well on her way to becoming an elite ballet dancer. But when her oldest friend, Donovan, returns home after spending four long years with his kidnapper, Theo starts reliving memories about his abduction--and his abductor. 
 Donovan isn't talking about what happened, and even though Theo knows she didn't do anything wrong, telling the truth would put everything she's been living for at risk. But keeping quiet might be worse. 
 What I Liked: 
 First, a HUGE thanks to Madeleine of MadnBooks, who traded this book for a copy of Throne of Glass (somehow, I ended up with one hardcover and three paperback copies of Throne of Glass. Now I just have the hardcover, which is signed, by the way. Yay for me not being a complete and utter glutton). I've really wanted to read this book, for about two years now, so when I saw this trade offer on YA Book Exchange, I was all over that. And Madeleine made the trade and shipped the book and I received it in like, less than two weeks! Fabulous. 
 Anyway. Book. It's obvious to readers from the beginning that something happened to Theo, and that she is still recovering from whatever it is that happened. We don't know what EXACTLY happened, or how Theo had to deal with the aftermath, but slowly, we see that it has to do with her eating habits. When Theo's friend and neighbor Donovan comes home after being missing (kidnapped) for four years, Theo's own ordeal surfaces. The two situations (for lack of a better word, forgive the insensitivity) are related, but it takes the most of the book to see how and why. 
 One of the things that I didn't quite realize when I first discovered this book is that it is a "tough-issues" book. This book is on of the Friday the Thirteeners book - the last debut to be published, might I add. I've read nine of the thirteen debuts, if anyone was wondering. But anyway. You all know that I'm not the biggest fan of contemporary novels, especially "tough-issue" contemporary novels. This one was a REALLY good one though, and this is coming from someone who doesn't really enjoy contemporary novels! 
 I'm not sure why this one worked so well for me. Perhaps it was the approach to the novel, to the "tough issue" (or the multitude of them), or the protagonist herself. Usually, with tough-issue novels, I HATE the protagonist, because her decisions and her logic generally makes no sense. Like, for example, NOT reporting rape or physical abuse. Or hurting yourself. I don't want to get started on these issues because yes, there is always a psychological explanation for everything. But this book features a different kind of story, and a different type of mindset. 
 I hope I don't spoil anything in this review. But Theo isn't the typical heroine that blames herself for everything and hurts herself and keeps quite because it's HER FAULT. She does keep quiet about what happened, but because she is completely convinced that nothing wrong occurred between her and a certain someone. She is completely convinced that what she was doing at age thirteen was okay, consensual, and right. What she agonized over was after he left. And then Donovan left/disappeared. And Theo suffered. She didn't eat, yet she continued to dance, to do her schoolwork, to pretend like everything was okay. It wasn't, and eventually, she was caught. 
 This book starts with Theo's After, after she went through a recovery period, after she was declared "better". It begins with Donovan's reappearance, and Theo's reaction to Donovan's reappearance as well as something else - something I won't give away. 
 I really like Theo. I already said that she is different from most heroines in similar situations (again, forgive the lack of sensitivity), and I mean that. Her naivete about what happened to her made me not want to shake her, and her personality in general was likable. I'm a very different person, but I like Theo, and we would get along. 
 Her passion for ballet is incredible. Of course, it drove her to do not-so-great things (which will not be mentioned), but I admire that type of passion. In my review of The Art of Lainey by Paula Stokes, I mentioned this passion towards soccer (sports in general). A close friend is a soccer player at JHU, and he definitely holds and harnesses this type of passion, towards soccer. It's remarkable and inspiring, how passionate a person can be about something, especially a sport or music or art or reading or some hobby. I love how well Colbert infused this passion for ballet into this book. I could feel like it in this book. 
 The story is twisted and tangled and messy, and I can't say anything specific without giving things away. I will say that I LOVE the structure of the plot. We get to see how things progress, in terms of developments with Donovan and the trial, but also with Theo's ballet, her returning bad eating habits, her love life, and also, her past. That's the thing I REALLY like - Colbert sprinkles scenes from the past throughout the book, so that we do not know everything about Theo's past all at once. We get bits and pieces, hints and clues, and we discover the full story as we read. I like this! 
 I mentioned Theo's love life... it's a bit of a mess. I didn't feel strongly towards any male in this book, in terms of romance (not saying that there are multiple potential males). There IS a presence of romance in this book, but I like the direction that Colbert took the romance. It definitely fit Theo's life in general, and the flow of the story. I'm satisfied with the ending, in terms of romance. 
 In general, the ending is PERFECT. Like, not cookie-cutter perfect, but imperfectly perfect. It fit Theo really well, it fits Donovan well, it just makes sense all around. I'm very hard on authors and ending, so it's rare that I'm all like YES THIS ENDING PASSES THE ALYSSA TEST. Heck, the same could be said about the book in general. It passes the Alyssa test! 
 What I Did Not Like: 
 Honestly? The only thing that really bothered me was the pacing of the first third of the book. It was slow, and I found my attention deviating. HOWEVER, now that I've finished the book, I recognize the need for the beginning to be slower. So I'm putting it as a "negative" thing because I want others to know that if you are stuck in the beginning, KEEP READING! 
 Would I Recommend It: 
 I would HIGHLY recommend this book, especially to contemporary! This is coming from someone who generally does not enjoy contemporary novels. Also, this is coming from ALYSSA, your harda** critic. So. It must be pretty good. 
 Rating: 
 4 stars. What an excellent debut! And a fine, lovely, heartbreaking contemporary novel, if you ask me. I cannot wait to read Colbert's next novels!

I enjoyed the first two books of the "Brilliance" trilogy, but "Written in Fire" fell a bit flat for me. The first two books do a good job of world-building, showing how the brilliants have influenced and changed the world and how the "normals" have worked to oppress them. With a variety of fresh and intriguing characters, as well as mixed media such as advertisements and social media, the first two books establish this world and the perils both brilliants and normals face. 
 "Written in Fire" is much more focused on Cooper and the militia, the New Sons of Liberty, that is determined to attack the New Canaan Holdfast, where many brilliants live. I've always found Cooper a bit annoying as the hero - he is *too* heroic, if you know what I mean, with a perfect family, an understanding ex-wife, a beautiful and talented lover. But in "Written in Fire," Cooper's self-righteousness is absurdly over the top, to the point where I kept rolling my eyes at his antics. I preferred the other POVs, especially Natalie and Owen Leahy, who are both intriguing characters. I liked that Sakey developed Natalie more, showing how a "regular" mom can become courageous under fire. 
 My biggest problem with the book was John Smith's absurd, villainous plan. So, so much of it did not make sense. If you want to make the country into brilliants, you don't need to provoke a war - just do what ended up happening anyway, and send a few people into different parts of the country with the virus. Smith's plans in the first two books made much sense than the final reveal in "Written in Fire." I also disliked that the story isn't really resolved. Was it really necessary to send Hawk - already a poorly developed character - out into the world to infect Americans with the brilliant virus? I assume we'll be getting more of Hawk in a future series - but I'm not sure I really will care enough to read it.  
 The climactic battle scene was fine, but I preferred the quieter moments in the series. I was a little disappointed that there had to be a final battle. But I did appreciate the metaphor of a militia of gun owners trying to take out people who they felt were "different." The best parts of the Brilliance trilogy are the subtle political commentary on the modern world, and Sakey does a good job using social media etc. to parallel social issues in today's world. 
 So, while there were a few glimpses of brilliance (ha, ha) in "Written in Fire," it was mostly an okay ending to the trilogy. If the book had been more like the first two, and showed a broader view of the world than just the New Canaan Holdfast, I think it would have provided a more full and fitting ending to an otherwise exciting trilogy.

In theory, I love this book. It's about the melding of cultures and how women interact with career and romance and it's a romance born from people not liking each other etc etc. I loved all those things about this book, but I just didn't feel like the execution followed through on those ideas as much as possible. There were some moments that were unbearably cliche, and I didn't think that the main characters were quite as developed as they could have been. That being said, the ideas are still impressive and the romance is pretty adorable. 
 Dimple is overjoyed that her parents have finally given up on finding her an "ideal Indian husband" and are letting her go to a coding competition for the summer. What she doesn't know is that Rishi, the boy her parents have secretly picked out as her future husband through an arranged marriage, is also going to the program, and he's totally excited about the possibility of marrying her. 
 Spoilers Discussion! 
 The romance was adorable, I'm not really going to debate that. The build was decent (I may have given it a tad bit longer, but in general it was pretty good) and they had some really cute moments. There was also the great switch in stereotypical gender roles where the girl is the one who wants a relationship and the boy is more hesitant. Also where the girl wants to go further sexually than the boy does. It was cute. 
 I also like that they did have sex (though of course we didn't get an explicit scene), because I think that's more realistic given the situation. Especially because they have a room to themselves when working/ practicing for the talent show etc. 
 I wish that Rishi's position on arranged marriage had been explained more. I think that there can be this really complex relationship between the culture of your parents and your culture, and I think that Dimple's position is explained a little bit more (or, at least, maybe it's easier for me to understand.) Rishi's position is kind of key to his whole character, and their whole dynamic, so not having his reasoning fleshed out too much more than he feels like he has to be good because of Ashish was kind of disappointing. 
 Okay, so when Celia comes off-stage and is talking about why she had to... It was the most cliche, least actual-teenager-speak series of sentences ever. We get what happened, Celia doesn't have to slip into after-school special voice to explain it all to us. I thought that plot-line was kind of juvenile from the beginning, especially because we don't have that background on Celia that says, "she was super uncool in high school." We're not inside her brain, so her motivations just seem stupid. Besides the part where Dimple says they can be friends without being friends with each other's friends (mouthful), that whole plotline was super lackluster. 
 I think that Dimple's struggles with defining herself as either someone with a career or with a significant other is super intriguing. She's smart and capable and also is really interested in this boy, and those things can all be true. 
 The writing was fine, I wish that it had been a little funnier or more lyrical or more something to give it some punch. As is, it was a way to tell the story, plain and simple, not part of the story, or a form of art, in and of itself. 
 The other thing with a competition is that it's kind of the easy way to end a story, it's a natural end/ climax. But, then you have to choose who is going to win, and I think it's hard to end a competition story in a way that feels real. Here, it was like a win without technically being a win, but the loss itself wasn't really that interesting. They lost because someone else had more money, which is a real thing that happens, but not super relevant to the other themes of the story. I didn't think they had to win or lose, really, but I wish it could've just been a program more about exploration than about winning. 
 I also thought that Ashish and Celia were definitely cute, but also a little unneeded? I don't know, the more that I think about this book, unfortunately, the less I like it. It's still not bad or anything by any means, but I think it could've put together a little bit more thoughtfully, beyond the original premise. 
 I don't have too much more to say. It definitely had its moments, but nothing really stood out about it either way. I will probably read more of Ms. Menon's work, especially if she continues to write about characters who we don't often see in YA. 
 Fin!

This book was picked for our office book club book for July, a pick that I'm glad about because I never would have read it otherwise. Cloud Atlas could be described as six interconnected novellas with a basic theme, but that's putting it in the most simplest terms. 
 The book is about a journey on sea, about a penniless young man working for a highly regarded composer, about a journalist treading over dangerous water to unveil the truth about an evil corporation, about a clone living in a not-so-distant dystopia, and about a post-apocalyptic society. So yes, this book covers a lot of ground and yes, it is epic, but everything is tied neatly together with the book's central theme.

It's good that that didn't stop me from reading this book because it's a wonderful book with a decent message. The narrative is strong, the characters are fleshed out, and the plots are intriguing. Best of all, each story is different enough from the next that I was surprised Mitchell could change his writing style so drastically, yet still tie the stories together with invisible strings. 
 I'm usually wary of books that are structured strangely just for the sake of conversation, but the frame within a frame, mirror structure of Cloud Atlas works so well it's almost as if the framing device is a complete character with its own quirks and behaviors. Reading the book is kind of like reading a mystery, only instead of the mystery unfolding linearly, it does so in a 3D space.

 I'll admit that darkness made me feel uneasy at times, but I think that's exactly what it was going for.

The book never waivers from this theory--this strange young man is definitely Ellie's grandfather. Props for that, but many of the intriguing questions from this set-up are left unanswered. As I was reading, I was disappointed thatEllie never comes across as an eleven-year-old girl. Her character is hard to pin down. She does start to grow into a budding scientist, though, and that transition is truly wonderful. The conclusion is highly resonant and appropriately thematic without ever seeming truly earned. The Fourteenth Goldfish is a fine experiment.

 Getting through this book took me a while, only because of the life stuff. I could have read this in one intense sitting, although I would definitely have sobbed had that been the case.  I have to start by talking about the dragons, because, ummm, dragons are freaking cool. Seraphina is pretty much what I was dreaming the book Firelight would be...only better. This one, too, has dragon shifters, but these are so much better thought out and so much more serious than Sophie Jordan's. This isn't about dragons just because paranormal's in; Seraphina focuses more on social tensions, bigotry, and prejudice. 
 The dragons here remind me most of Vulcans. They live their lives based on logic and find emotions to be in bad taste. However, one of the most fascinating aspects is how shifting to human form can affect their brains, breeding improper emotions like love and hatred. There was also a scary aspect, since any dragon found guilty of undue emotion was likely to get his/her dragon brain wiped of all memories, so that the human taint could be removed. 
 As may be obvious, there is a lot of tension between humans and dragons (whether in human form or not), despite the treaty that has created a tentative alliance between the two species. These tensions are seriously close to erupting after the murder (possibly by a dragon) of one of the countries princes. An anti-dragon group , the Sons of Ogdo, is constantly gaining in adherents. Meanwhile, the dragons obviously view humans with some amount of contempt, both for their emotions and their brief lifespans. 
 In this world, humans and dragons (while in human form...there is no bestiality up in here) are forbidden from forming romantic attachments and, most especially, from procreating. Well, as with rules, this one has been broken. Seraphina discovers in her youth that she is half-dragon. Her father did not know, in fact, that his wife was a dragon until she died in childbirth, her silver blood spilling from her body. Seraphina has red blood, but she also has scales along her stomach, back and arms. She leaves her life trying to avoid notice, a lonely life with only her tutor and uncle, Orma, for a friend. 
 Despite her need for anonymity, she cannot keep quiet when she begins to suspect she knows the answers to some of the mystery surrounding the prince's death. She finds herself having to choose between her country's best interests and her own, between loneliness and love. Seraphina is an amazingly strong, wonderful heroine. I loved her for her faults as well as her skills and cleverness; she lies constantly, even when the truth might be better, and she has serious trust issues. She is, however, braver than just about anyone. 
 Seraphina was DAMN close to being a perfect five star read for me. The only aspect that I continually found jarring, even though Hartman did explain it and it did work, was Seraphina's mental garden. This won't really make sense if you haven't read the book, but you'll get it when you do. I personify things, including my brain, picturing it filled with disordered shelves covered in dust, often locked with now wayward keys. That's probably a little weird, or even a lot. Seraphina's relationship with her mind, though, makes mine pale in comparison. It was just a bit too weird for me, and the descriptions perhaps ran a bit long. It was the only part of the book that dragged at all for me. 
 This book seems to me like Firelight (for the dragon shifters) + Cinder (girl who has to hide what she is, affecting her relationships) + a whole lot more awesomeness that is all Rachel Hartman's. The writing and the world building are both completely exceptional. I am already salivating for the sequel and the title hasn't even been released yet. I declare myself to be, based on just this novel, a firm Hartman fan.

Slaughterhouse-Five is an extremely unique book. I had a strong love-hate relationship with it. I loved the writing, theme, and entire concept of this story. However, I also thought it was a little boring and all over the place at times. But in the end, I believe it had some beautiful, human moments. Some of the passages were brilliant. It was those parts that I loved, which pushed the rating up for me. I had to read this for a Banned Books class I'm taking in college, but I was intending on getting around to it sometime anyway. It's pretty good, and I'm glad that I read it. 
 I listened to the audiobook, which again was kind of a good and a bad thing. The audiobook version makes some of the repetition and boring parts of the novel come to life. The narrator does a great job of conveying the tone of the work, which I'm not sure would translate as well if you just read the physical copy. However, if you get distracted AT ALL while listening to audiobooks, this one might not be for you. Because each chapter is so jumbled and jumps around, if you zone out for like 30 seconds, the scene has already shifted to something else. Sometimes I felt as if it was hard to understand the timeline of the story and everything that was happening. I'm not entirely sure if that was an issue with the book or just a result of listening to the audio version. I might go back and re-read the physical edition sometime. 
 I'm not gonna go into the plot of this one too much, since it's so well-known. Essentially, Billy Pilgrim was an American soldier who witnessed the bombing of Dresden. He believes that he has come unstuck in time, so he is constantly visiting different points of his life. On top of that, he gets abducted by aliens. They put him on display in a type of zoo, but still occasionally let him return home, so no one worries that he's gone missing. I liked the plot well enough. My favorite parts were definitely those revolving around the Tralfamadorian aliens. They had a very different point of view, and I loved reading about it. The war parts kind of dragged on after a while. It's a war book, so maybe I shouldn't be complaining. But eventually, I understood the point, and got bored of it. 
 This isn't going to be too long of a review. I'm sleepy, but wanted to update this book on my shelves. I might go back and and edit this later. But all in all, I enjoyed Slaughterhouse-Five. It's a confusing little piece of literature, but I'm assuming that's how Vonnegut intended it to be. The anti-war message is strong and there are some philosophical bits that make you think. There are also some really clever sections, if you pay attention-- for example, Vonnegut inserts himself into the novel in numerous chapters, which was cool. Slaughterhouse-Five is definitely worth picking up. I would recommend that everyone reads it once.

 Barbara is a character that I continuously had to remind myself to not judge too harshly. I figured there had to be an explanation. And there is...I'm just not sure it's enough. She's not nice, she's abusive and mean, and there's nothing in these pages that excuses that behavior - though many people make excuses for her behavior. However, there are reasons for her actions, too. It doesn't make them right, but she's an 11 (or so) year old child and even adults don't always react in the best possible way to difficult circumstances. 
 The author took an interesting angle of not allowing us to know what exactly is going on with Barbara, and not letting us find out until nearly the very end. I went into this book expecting a good fantasy, slaying, giant-killing story. And that's what I got, but on a different level. We, each of us, have giants to slay, things to overcome, and I think children have some of the most difficult ones as they learn how to navigate all the different, and sometimes painful, realities of life. 
 So, while I absolutely detested some - or a lot - of the things that Barbara did, it's hard to judge her. Because I understand, too. She takes her pain and anger out on those around her, not always justly, not fairly, but it's an emotional reaction that she can't quite control yet. 
 If I could have wished for one thing, it would have been her getting called on the behavior a bit more. The story dealt with getting her to deal with the underlying issue, and that's definitely needed, but I think that if we don't check ourselves when we're in pain and angry, care and empathy can get away from us - and it's a good lesson for kids that might be reading this to learn. 
 As I tell my son, nothing excuses violence - and believe me, it's a fine line to walk teaching no violence and the right to defend yourself. That's something I would have appreciated seeing reinforced here. When I started this, in the first dozen or so pages, I was going to pass it on to my daughters' to read. Now, I think I'm going to pass. Because no matter how much I can understand Barbara's pain, I can't excuse her violent responses to non-violent circumstances, or hurtful language - especially in a time when such things are so prevalent as it is. 
 There were a couple of things - beyond the violence that I mentioned above - that really bothered me here: 1) the comment from Barbara to her PE teacher (calling the teacher a "bull dyke"), this book would have been much more highly rated. But that's a line I wasn't comfortable with, especially when it was never, ever addressed or recriminated. Honestly, the more I think about it, the madder I get; 2) "fat girl bully"; 3) "I'm not like other girls, other girls are stupid"; 4) the boy/girl interests divide - can we just have a book that shows it's okay to like whatever one wants to like and not disparage others for liking other things? Ugh. 
 The more I write my review, the more I dislike what I've read. And that's just the story. I also didn't find the art particularly engaging - most of the time I had a hard time figuring out what was going on. I think that's a stylistic choice to fit with the fantasy/reality divide that we're straddling, but it didn't work for me.

Just when you think you have this book figured out, you find out that you actually don't. Which is one of the more frustrating things ever! I like to support Canadian authors, but it can be kinda hard when the books they come out with are a little hard to get through because of how little sense they make. While I was able to make some sense of this book, it was a little out there at times. 
 This book is about Romy Grey, a girl who used to be best friends with the pretty, popular girl. Then she got raped by the town's golden boy, the sheriff and town hero's son. Because she speaks out, she becomes the most hated girl in town. Romy is still struggling to deal with this while being tortured by her classmates, the friends of her rapist. She's sure that no one will ever believe her when her ex-BFF tries to help her. But then she and Romy go missing at the same time and only Romy comes back within a couple hours. 
 At times, this book was quite confusing. I had a hard time figuring out what was happening in the present and past during this book. Some of the character relationships also threw me off. I didn't realize that Kellan and Alek were related until probably half way through the book. Some things were explained all that much either. I was left to assume why Romy was obsessive about her red nail polish and lipstick. And Romy would call her past self her sometimes, but however, it was hard to figure out when the her was Romy or someone else. (maybe I was reading a little fast though) 
 This book was just really dark. Kinda puts a damper on the whole "new year, new beginning" thing happening right now. This book is about rape and this book is set in a small town, where everyone talks. You can probably see where this is going. Throughout this book, Romy is seriously bullied. Think situations like her underwear gets stolen and she is forever called a slut. 
 I think the most interesting parts were with Romy. Her outlook on life was very interesting and kinda sad. She believes that no one will believe her anymore and that she has to take care of herself so she always lies to everyone. (which, was super annoying at times but I kinda get it) The book is worth a read just to get into the head of a rape victim, to see how it feels to be blamed for something that wasn't your choice. 
 I was a little mad with the ending because it left a lot to interpretation but with a book this like, I had no clue how it could end either. The romance in this book made me mad, but I think that was because of Romy more than anything. Because she was raped and has been bullied immensely because of it, she has a lot of barriers that someone who wants to be with her would have to break down. Romy, in this book, tries to be in a relationship to get out of her head but her head also fights her. It was really frustrating to read, but again, can I really blame her? Nope. 
 I would recommend this book if you're looking for something that's a little dark but VERY realistic and has a lot of depth. There are some interesting ideas brought up in this book that you might find really eye opening.

At which point I realized that was a SUPER western, American lens to be looking through. The point of the book wasn't to subvert anything; it was a cute romcom about characters navigating their Indian identities and how they feel about their families' expectations. So they end up happily together, no subversion, because the book isn't meant to be read within that lens. Which is why it was important for me, as a white American reader, to a) read it, b) realize where that expectation had come from, and c) let go of it. 
 #OwnVoices is really important for people getting to see themselves, but a side benefit is that people like me -- with privilege -- get a reminder that the world is much wider than our privilege would lead us to believe, and we need to remember to look beyond what we know.  
 Anyway, really fun!

I really enjoyed this book! It was very silly and hard to sympathise with the protagonist at times, but I grew to love this story and all of its characters. 
 Our protagonist, Poppy Wyatt, is about to marry her dream man. In one day, she manages to lose both her engagement ring (a family jewel) and her phone (which is her entire life!). She finds a discarded phone inside a trash bin, says 'finders keepers' and uses it to try to track down the ring and save herself from the embarrassment of facing her in-laws. But she finds that the phone's owner is less than thrilled to have her poking about his personal life. Hilarity ensues. 
 What I like about this story is that it is funny. It had me laughing out loud at times. I also liked that Poppy is very 'normal'. She's not overly pretty, she's smart but not scholarly level, and she sometimes acts in ways that make you cringe. That is what makes this book so fun to read. You can practically insert yourself into the silly romance, because she is so relatable. I also can relate to her in the way that she has a hard time with confrontation and tends to let people walk all over her because she wants to be well-liked. I think we all can relate, yes? 
 On the other hand, because Poppy is so normal, I found myself getting annoyed easily. Some of the decisions she made were just embarrassing.  Especially when it came to the emails she sent out on Sam's behalf. The second hand embarrassment was strong! All of this can be redeemed because their banter by the end of the book was so cute, I was swooning more than cringing.  
 I would recommend this book to anyone who is a fan of contemporary romances. It had me laughing out loud and there is nothing too heavy.

During the years that I was in the Boy Scouts I also devoured horror novels by the truckload. The post-Stephen King horror boom was just beginning to wane a little bit, and the splatter-punk crowd (Skipp & Spector, Barker, etc) was just coming into their own. 21st century references aside, The Troop reads exactly as if it came from that period and my 14 year old self would have scarfed every word down and passed around the plate for seconds. The novel is economical, sharp, and it has a powerful engine which runs on nothing but fear and revulsion. 
 Five scouts and their Scoutmaster are taking their annual hiking trip on an uninhabited island just north of Prince Edward Island. Soon after they arrive a ghastly looking stranger appears, and . . . dear lord, is he hungry! For fans of a good horror tale, that's all you really need to know about the plot. I will add that the novel is goretastic. 
 The characters all straddle the fine line between archetypal and stereotypical. I find they land in the former category more often than the latter, and the novel is all the richer for it. This sense of modern archetypes testing their defined roles against extraordinary situations gives the novel a fable like quality I appreciate. The scoutmaster is a lonely middle aged man whose work with the troop provides the lion's share of his social activity. Kent is the jock, possibly a decent kid if his sense of entitlement didn't often cast him in the role of bully. Newton is the nerd, the soft one, the perpetual victim. Shelley is the cryptic one, the budding sociopath straight out of the serial killer chic novels of the early 90's. Ephraim and Max are updates of Bradbury's James Nightshade and William Halloway, best friends one of whom is from a troubled family and struggles with being better, the other a kid from a loving family just beginning to feel the attraction of the dark side. All of these characters have their individual quirks and struggles, but unlike many of the reviewers I've read here I find their archetypal qualities to be a benefit rather than a detriment to the story. Oh, I almost forgot Mr Padgett, the stranger, he's just hungry. 
 I recommend this novel to horror afficionados who recognize that the abject, or gross-out if you prefer, has a place in a writer's repertoire. All others need not apply. 
 Note: This novel contains a large amount of cruelty towards animals. This comes in three forms: the sociopath who does it for fun, the mad scientist who does it in the name of his perverted ideals, and a couple of the protagonists who do it accidentally because they are not skilled at hunting. I find that all of these instances make sense and have their place in the novel, but recognize that many folk will find these passages hard to take.

 All right, I'm not getting anything else done, and a nap seems to be eluding me, so here goes. 
 I had a devilish hard time reading this book. I just couldn't connect with the writing at all. I found it extremely dry and explain-y, and my mind would wander any time there wasn't dialogue. Which was, ah, most of the time. 
 Now I have to say: I think this is my fault too, and not just the book's. Sometimes a writing style just doesn't connect with my thinking style, and that isn't anybody's fault. I really need characters to connect to, and 3rd person omniscient keeps you at arm's length. That said, it's good for much of what she was trying to do, which is action. 
 I am probably in a minority here, but I tend to skim action. I find it blindingly tedious. Especially when it isn't even human action but somebody piloting a shuttlecraft into the airlock, or bullets whizzing around. *snore* 
 Much of this book just wasn't my thing. The parts that MIGHT have been my thing kept feeling muted and truncated. For example: Waverly having invasive, non-consensual, egg-stealing surgery. Her reaction to that was so... nothing? Or maybe it was all done in explain-y writing and I zoned out. I dunno. Same with Kieran being starved. I felt like the author had done a LOT of research on what happens to your body when you're starved, but somehow the effect felt really clinical to me, and not so horrifying. . I came very close to putting this down for good many times because I just wasn't feeling it. 
 Absurdly, everything that came in the book's "Epilogue", I found much more interesting and compelling than what had gone before. Trauma changing people? PTSD reaction to religion? Philosophical implications of what Kieran has been up to? Sign me up! 
 And then, of course, the book was done. Huh. Will I read the next one? Dunno. Maybe, if I read some reviews that convince me we're getting inside the characters a bit more, and not just scraping our shuttlecrafts across the hard metallic surface of the world.

Aoife (pronounced like "Eva" only with an "f" instead of a "v", in case you were wondering)is positive that she is going to go mad when she reaches the age of 16. Her mother did and continues to languish in one of Lovecraft's many sanatoriums. Her brother did as well. Right before he came at Aoife with a knife. To be mad is to be considered contagious. The "necrovirus" has been spreading insanity for so long that the local government is obsessed with keeping it (and any heresy, meaning anything that is not rational and therefore connected) as far away as it can. One day, Aoife gets a message from her missing brother, telling her to head for their father's house in Arkham. Aoife feels that her estranged father might have the answer to preventing madness so she grabs her friend Cal and breaks out of Lovecraft in pursuit of her family's secrets. Along the way, they pick up a guide named Dean who decides to stick it out with them until the end. The house in Arkham contains a library which opens the doors to more than Aoife ever thought possible. 
 There is so much going on in this book and so many themes, it can be hard to wrap one's head around at times. Aoife's world is brutal and mechanical; arts, magic and philosophy are strictly forbidden. It's also set sometime in the mid-twentieth century (much later than I had originally suspected), but the societal attitudes seem even more didactic. The world doesn't always make sense, particularly the necrovirus. It's not just that though, things start to get really weird around the time Aoife and co. make it to Arkham. As it turns out, everything prohibited as fanciful "heresy" is dangerous reality. An ambitious book that combines alternate history, totalitarian governments, steampunk aesthetics, fairy curses, multiple "worlds", and lots of strange creatures that can don human form with mixed results. The pace lags at times and the plot is slightly convoluted, but there's sure to be an audience for this one.

 #2: Cricket. I hated her. I mean, I really don't know why. I was irritated at how indecisive and unsure she was all the time.

 It was disappointing. 
 #4: I hated the parts where Piper would feature in Spencer's nightmares. They were stupid and highly unnecessary. 
 #5: This is the most important point. 
 Spencer Blackwell in NOT Greed. 
 Piper is Greed.

 I love Fisher Amelie. And I'd probably be reading Fury, the next book.

 And three stars??

"Had our hearts really become so numb that we needed dead bodies in order to feel the beat of compassion in our chests? Who am I if I need to be shocked back into my best self?" 
 This book hit me pretty hard. The dual narration between Rashad and Quinn allowed for topics to be discussed from different sides, which is so important for the topics raised in the book. Rashad regularly broke my heart with how strong he was in the face of the media attention and his fear. To see him go beyond his own self and realize that what happened to him was about so much more than that one terrible night really hit home. When the names of the killed black kids were being read during the protest, tears came to my eyes when I realized that the names they used weren't fictional. Hearing those names that I've heard on the news in this context, even though this story is fiction, really affected me.  
 Quinn's slow realization of his unintentional racism was eyeopening. Being white, it really made me think about how I view the world and how I react to the news. His relationship with Paul put him in a very difficult position, and I felt how following his heart was a real struggle. I liked that they didn't make it easy for him, though I think that his acceptance of these difficult topics happened rather quickly. But intense pressure can produce intense results, and the combined force of his relationship with Paul's family, basketball, and his eyewitness account of the incident combined to really put Quinn on the spot. 
 This book isn't without flaws, though. The writing isn't amazing and sometimes characterization was pushed to the background to make room for the important issues. Paul felt very flat as a character, despite being so central to the plot. The bit about Rashad's dad shooting that kid years ago felt very out of nowhere and I don't think it really contributed to the plot. It just felt like a set piece to discuss how good cops make mistakes. I think this could have been better painted through Paul, but the narrative make him a flat antagonist. Which I understand, as that his how things can be in the real world. But it didn't make for a fulfilling story in that regard.  Rashad and Quinn were very well developed, but the rest of the cast was, like I said, left underdeveloped to focus on the issues. 
 And these issues are important. Ultimately, I think everyone should read this book. It is pretty short and pretty powerful. Don't expect literary excellence here, but expect to think and to feel. As a librarian, I wish that the swearing wasn't so prominent so I could more easily recommend this to middle grade readers. This book was just amazing. 
 It definitely had one of the greatest starts I've ever read. It began with Cole, one of our MCs and a PI, running from a septuagenarian in a leather bikini and a shotgun because Cole caught her with her lesbian lover. Picture something like this running at you with a shotgun: 
 (If my and Cole's retinas had to burn, then I think it's only fair that yours do too!) XD 
 If that beginning doesn't grab, I don't know what will! *snickers* 
 But, seriously, this book was just awesome. The writing was absolutely phe-nom-e-nal!!! This book was told from Cole's POV, and it was utterly entertaining, thoroughly engaging, full of witty one-liners, and just plain hilarious! 
 Here are a few examples of Cole's zingers (Trust me: there are plenty!): 
 A thick bristle of black hair stood out on his square head. It was so much like Mike's and Hyung-Shik's haircuts, I almost asked him if it was just a number you picked on a menu at the stylis, but the grim set of his face gave me pause. 
 She was back before I could turn over, tenderizing my body for what I was certain would be her midmorning snack. Being evil took a lot of energy, and something as small as she was probably had to keep up her strength. 
 "It's like a bad joke over here: a black woman, a Filipino transvestite, and a Korean ex-stripper walk into a gay man's house. All that's missing is a priest and a talking dog." 
 I just freakin' love Cole; he is just an amazing character! He is sarcastic, brash, and definitely thinks before he speaks. But he is also extremely caring and tender toward the people he loves. Jae-Min, our other MC, is also a very interesting character, and you can't help but feel sorry for him. He is hated by his family members who know that he is gay and treated like complete trash. He was forced to become a stripper at a Korean gay club just to make ends meet. In order to protect himself, Jae, understandably, finds it very hard to trust others and can appear cold. But, underneath, it is very obvious that he is hurting and just wants somebody to care for him. And thankfully, Cole sees that. These two are just an amazing couple. I am definitely going to continue reading about their story! 
 Also, the mystery/crime aspect of this novel was very well-done. The descriptions of the crime scenes were not gruesome per se, but they were illustrative enough to get a clear picture. I liked that the author did not gloss over the depictions of the crime scene; I liked knowing what Cole was seeing. It could just be me (I was never really very good at playing Clue), but I did not figure out the whodunnit until it was revealed. However, even though the mystery/crime subplot was, of course, very important to the story, I did not feel that it overshadowed the developing relationship between Cole and Jae. It was all a very nice blend. Even though there were only 3 sex scenes between the MCs, I did not feel that the romantic aspect of the novel was missing at all. Like I said, the author did a great job in splitting the novel between the romance and the crime.
