"For you, my love, I would endeavor to pluck the stars from the sky, only to shower them at your feet." 
 I love this series and I will be honest and say that this is the one series that I have reread more than any. I appreciated how multi- faceted it was. It not only portrays a story of reconnecting between lost souls of Dante and Beatrice but it also talks of an astounding love between a family while also bringing literature and the arts and even religion into light as well. 
 In Gabriel's Redemption, we find the couple married and enjoying marital bliss. After the trials that they've been through in the first and second book you would think that everything in their relationship to be perfect but it isn't so. Gabriel is far more mature and accomplished in his career while Julianne is just starting to build a name for herself. While there is no competition between them their ideas in their field of study that they are both passionate about do differ. This is not something that comes easy for Gabriel - to be more supportive rather than argumentative when his once student brings new ideas to the table. 
 "It's hard for me to be a student in the same field as you. I always feel as if I'm always trying to catch up." 
 Given that Gabriel is so much older and that he his now content and happy in their marriage his priorities also have changed. He wants nothing more than to start a family with Julianne but she is not at that point in life. She is torn between achieving her dreams versus giving her husband what he wants most in the world. The guilt is eating at her and the one time she meets with Paul all those feeling and emotions swirling their friendship emerge and come to the surface. 
 " I'm not waiting in the wings. But it's hard for me to see you with him..." 
 The story does not only revolve between the couple which was unexpected for me. Christa once again shows her obnoxious side and is still trying to capture the professors attention. We also get a glimpse into the life of the other couples in the series such as Scott and Tammy, Rachel and Aaron and surprisingly Tom and Diane. Richard also played a vital role in this story. He was very supportive. Since he once experienced that deep connection with his Grace his advice to the newlyweds was moving and inspiring. 
 "...learning to fight fairly is an art, not a science. It took your mother and me a long time to figure it out. But once we did, we rarely argued. And when we did it wasn't hurtful. If you argue with Julia while still convincing her that you love her and that she's important to you, your conflicts will be easier to manage." 
 Through it all they learn to compromise and grow together. Despite their differences, the heated intellectual debates and their quarrels their love remains so profound, their past and present is so tightly intertwined, their connection so deep they can conquer anything as long as they are together. (Oh yeah, don't let me forget to mention that the make up sex is always AMAZING!) 
 As a reader one of my goals is to find that one story that talks of true love and this series definitely delivers what I am looking for. How the author was able to capture every emotion explicitly is remarkable. Nothing compares to Gabriel and Julia's story of reconnecting with your soul mate and in my opinion it will be years before another comes along to top this one.

The concept for this story was amazing! I love anything time travel, and I was impressed with the notion of a branch of the military assigned to monitoring historical events and alteration of them. Very cool! It's definitely not like any other time travel book out there. 
 I found the setup of the Annum Guard fascinating! The Annum watches were totally awesome! I liked their system of code names, too: Numbers for first generation, Greek alphabet for second, and colors for the third generation. 
 I liked Iris a lot, because I found that I identified with her. She made the best decisions she could, and to her, they made sense. Her heart was in the right place. But when Yellow accused her of being selfish, I was kind of taken aback. I agreed with Iris's decisions and thought they were founded; I didn't see them as selfish. But when Yellow explained it, it made sense. I could really relate to that, because I think very similar to the way Iris does. Family first, no matter what. I didn't see it as selfish to put her father before others (that weren't even her friends). 
 I have to admit though, Yellow earned my grudging respect. She's a bit of a snob, and in the beginning I hated her. She was a complete bitch to Iris (not to mention she was very judgmental), and I wanted to slap the shit out of her. Her snide remark about Iris not fitting into the dress pissed me off! But after she teamed up with Iris (unwillingly), I started to see her differently. Despite being forced together, they slowly became friends and started depending on each other. I loved that! And in the end, Yellow wasn't as bad as I thought she was. 
 Iris actually being part of Annum by blood was an interesting twist! I didn't see that one coming! I actually like that she realized her mother was actually trying to protect her all those years, and that she judged her too harshly. Goes to show that things aren't always as they seem!  
 I loved the concept, the aspect of time travel, and Iris's character, but there was still something missing for me that kept me from giving this book a higher rating. I'm not really sure what it is, I can't put my finger on it. Maybe it just felt too short? Which is silly, because the audio was 11 hours long. I think some of it just felt rushed and underdeveloped, but like I said, I can't pinpoint why. I also didn't connect as well as I'd hoped. While I loved Iris, I didn't get much feeling from this story. My emotional slate while reading (listening) was pretty blank, I'm afraid. 
 The Audio 
 I chose this book for audio specifically because it was Amy McFadden narrating. She narrated The Darkest Minds and I was highly impressed by how well she did. I'm sad to say that she didn't wow me as much in this one. I had trouble telling the difference between the characters sometimes because her voice didn't change very much (which was so NOT the case with Darkest Minds!!). I also couldn't tell that she was actually saying "Alpha" until they introduced the other Guard members with Greek alphabet names. I seriously thought the guy's name was "Elpha" because that's how she pronounced it. I wasn't really a fan of her narration at all for this book, despite how amazing she was at narrating The Darkest Minds.

I got my Elizabeths mixed up when I picked this book up off the new books shelf at the library--I was thinking Elizabeth Berg, not Elizabeth Lowell. This book was interesting and thorough in its background and world-building--the life of contracted boat owners and treasure hunters diving the Caribbean for gold and gems from long-sunk privateers--but the background was a foil for the love story, which was entered into abruptly, occurred at breathtaking speed, and resolved too neatly for my taste. Likewise the main character's journey from traumatized and in denial to competent and fearless was a bit much to believe. I also figured out who the bad guy was early on, simply by paying attention to a character the author was elaborately neglecting to develop. It wasn't bad--but it won't make me pursue other books of Lowell's either. I actually think I read one of her early books and liked it better--Midnight at Ruby Bayou.

This book was one of those perfect reading experiences because I had already come to terms with the style -- which in a broad sense is not typically to my taste -- during the first book, so I could dive into this fully prepared and ready to enjoy the characters and dialogue (which I think was even snappier than in the first). It was very satisfying on all counts. Locke and Jeanne set off on another one of their cons, and in the process find themselves living as pirates. 
 One odd thing is that the author has been pretty forthcoming in interviews and such about his own struggles with depression and anxiety (and my understanding is that this in part why the series seems to be quite slow) ... and it was weird to read this book with that knowledge. I get that plenty of authors suffer from depression, and that most fiction is informed in some way by emotional experiences of its author, but in this book in particular, Locke's feelings of guilt, despair, and fear of betrayal felt extremely personal to the extent that I felt vaguely bad about enjoying it so much.

4.5 stars 
 Overall, I really loved the book. The writing was really, really good. It is really hard to do a review on this book without giving away big spoilers, so I think I am going to focus mainly on the characters. This really is a character driven series! 
 Lena--I felt I connected more with Lena in this story than in the previous two books. I really felt her pain, in being torn between Alex and Julian, and then her pain in thinking Alex no longer loved her! 
 Alex--He was the biggest bummer of the book for me. I will defend him somewhat. He is obviously insanely jealous, and who knows what he went through in the Crypts. (Well, I do, because I read the short story "Alex!") But he was a horrible jerk to Lena through most of the book, and seemed to latch onto a new girl! I was happier with him by the end, though. 
 Hana--This character was the hardest for me to make sense of. I can't believe Hana's actions towards the end of the book. She seems to be coming around for most of the story, then she's threatened, and BAM--becomes a meek little mouse. It really helped me to read her short story, as well! 
 Raven--I wasn't a big fan of hers in Pandemonium, but I started to like her by the end. Again, her short story will shed a lot of light on her as a person. And there is a huge twist with her that is not even mentioned in Requiem, only her short story. I was crying at the end of the book for Raven! 
 Julian--Julian is the only character who no longer really has a purpose. I suppose it helps Lena that he's there, but a lot of Lena's problems would be gone if he wasn't there in the first place... 
 Annabel--Annabel makes an appearance in this book, and I'm really glad the author tied up things between Lena and Annabel. I figured we would never see her again, but I'm so glad I was wrong! Another really good short story to read! 
 Tack--We never get any closure on Tack, so I'm going to believe that he stayed with Raven. I honestly think Raven and Tack were the best couple of the whole series! So loyal and faithful to each other! 
 Fred--I'm not sure I've ever felt so venomous towards a character before! I'm not going to tell you what happens to this despicable creature, but he gets his in the end! 
 Coral--One of the new characters, whom I decided not to like for Lena's sake. I had come around by the end though. Its hard to hate someone who has lost everything! She also was the only character who could and did fix one of Lena's biggest issues! 
 There are so many other characters, but these are the ones that stick out for me. Oliver is an amazing writer, and she makes these characters come to life! I'm not going to go into too much with the plot, but I was completely engaged with it. 
 Now for the ending. I've heard lots of negative reviews on the ending, and I know why. Oliver gives us a pretty open ending, letting us figure out exactly happens with the characters after the big battle. I think her readers really wanted everything tied up in a nice little bow. My only complaint is I would have liked a little more closure with Julian, Hana, and Tack. The rest I can imagine on my own. 
 I, however, really LOVED the ending! The last page was beautiful. It was pure poetry, and one of the best things I have ever read! Lena sums up the series and its purpose beautifully, and its something we should all be thinking about every day of our lives!

I absolutely love the film, and so we started the book. As one would expect, it has a great "muchness" (thanks, Hatter/Depp) than the movie has, with nice details on Inigo, Fezzik, Prince Humperdinck, and Buttercup. And yet, while I would rate the film a high four, I am giving the book only a solid three. This is, chiefly, because they are really different things. 
 The film I love represents a pure, idealistic children's tale story-book adventure. It's a simple, old genre, but done with such flare, purity, and character that it lives endlessly in the memory of many fans. The book has at least as much flare and character; however, it is NOT a children's fairy tale. Rather, it is satiric almost to the point of slap stick in a world so intentionally crossed by the author's constant interjections, contradictions, and random elaborations that it is difficult to get any fixed point on the time, place, or how serious to take anything in the book. At the end, I only knew one thing--we had swords, boats, blue jeans, and public schools. 
  
 For those not in the know, the references to the original author Morganstern are all a gimmick (more kindly, a literary device). In addition to the story movie-lovers are familiar with, which is evidently not Goldman's first priority in this book, Goldman establishes a mock-dialogue between a false self (complete with imagined psychiatrist wife) and the Florin (also imaginary) satirist/original author Morganstern; this, evidently, is the central focus of the author, and not any tale of swords, wits, courage, and true love. Placed side-by-side, Goldman struck me as, at best, poking fun and, at worst, outright mocking the very things we love the movie for.  
 It isn't a bad book, and many people have loved it; however, it is not at all the same kind of story as the movie. Who would I recommend it to? To those who enjoy quirky, anachronistic satire a la Dave Barry. Who might enjoy it less? Those who want to get immersed in a story of romantic fantasy adventure.

Mr and Mrs Dursley, of number four, Privet Drive, were proud to say that they were perfectly normal, thank you very much. They were the last people you'd expect to be involved in anything strange or mysterious, because they just didn't hold with such nonsense. 
 Just from this paragraph, even if you hadn't bothered to read the back of the book, you knew something strange or mysterious is going to happen. And it did. Thus began the tale of Harry Potter, the hero of the greatest saga ever written (in my humble opinion). 
 Harry is an orphan (yes that is cliche), and lives with his horrible relatives, the Dursleys. He soon finds out he isn't who he thought he was ('gasp'!) and is whisked off to Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry for a magical and sometimes dangerous education. 
 What makes it so absolutely amazing: 
 - The characters: Every character is so unique and fleshed out, with a very distinct personality, strengths and weaknesses . Every single individual we meet has a signature 'something', be it the glasses, scar and impossible hair or Dumbledore's piercing eyes and long white beard. The characters manage to be over the top without seeming to try hard to be so, so they come across as natural even while wearing floor length robes or being twice the size of a normal person. Best characters in book one: Harry (of course), though he doesn't come to his potential into book two when he stops feeling like just an observer and more of the real hero. Ron: funny, loyal and red-headed :) Ron is Harry's best friend and a master at wizard chess. Hermione: in the beginning she is just so annoying! the best part of her story is to watch her grow from the girl we first meet to the girl who would break the rules to help her friends. Hagrid: The friendly giant (half-giant, actually), Hagrid will win you over with his sweet personality and love for all things creature (spoiler: giant-three headed dogs and illegal dragons are just some of those animals he loves). Honorable mentions: Dumbledore, Professor McGonagall, Snape, Dudley, Uncle Vernon, Aunt Petunia, Quirrell, Neville, Draco. 
 - The plot: Again, the perfect word for Harry Potter is unique. Though the simplest plot of all seven books, Sorcerer's Stone still manages to keep you turning the pages uncontrollably. 
 - The locations: From Diagon Alley in London, to Hogwarts castle in Scotland, every location Harry visits jumps off the page with absolute clarity and again, uniqueness. 
 - The details: The pages are just filled with amazing details and interesting facts about the wizarding world making it come alive and feel very real. 
 - It's hilarious: Harry Potter is one of the rare books that aren't 'funny' books, yet make you laugh anyway. The Dursleys are extremely funny in their effort to be 'normal' which they fail at horrendously. The best part about the comedy is that there are little lines here and there that are hilarious, yet fit into the page like they are totally normal and not going out of their way to be funny. Ex: ""No post on Sundays," he (Uncle Vernon) reminded them happily as he spread marmalade on his newspapers." pg. 34-35. I love this line since it so easily goes unnoticed, since he's just spreading marmalade. I read this aloud to my little brother and he didn't notice what it said, until a second later when he realized and he was like 'What?' and burst out laughing. 
 - The fact that it can combine all kinds of themes and totally work. Magic, adventure, suspense, comedy, a kids story that adults love, romance (not yet, but you just wait), friendship, family, belonging, death, etc etc. The best books are the ones that can span all borders and categories they are boxed into, and this is one book that does so extremely well. 
 My few complaints (since this is an honest review) 
 - The writing: JK is a story teller and it shows. Luckily, I can tell you that her writing style and prose greatly improves over the course of seven books, which shows even the best writers need improvement.

Sarah Dessen has ruined my romantic expectations, and she'll probably ruin yours too. 
 It all started with Dexter of This Lullaby fame. Oh, Dexter. It's been years, and I still remember the butterflies I had in my young teenage stomach when reading about Dexter playing the guitar shirtless, Dexter doing ridiculous things that concerned tupperware, Dexter winning the heart of the oh-so-cold Remy. 
 Then there was Wes. Ah, yes. Many a girl has fallen prey to Wes, who runs around shirtless (shirtlessness is very important to me) and earns sah-woons from hapless females. Yet despite the fact that he probably looks kind of like Adonis, Wes isn't a douche about it. Wes will play word games with you and Wes will be there and Wes is great okay. 
 Owen. Ah, somewhat controversial Owen. I know that some people found Just Listen to be a bit of a Speak ripoff, but I disagree. Mainly because of Owen and his "fuck you" knuckle tattoos ("or not") and magical car washes that include kissing. And the distinct sense you get that a guy like Owen will pound someone bloody into the pavement for you, and to be honest, that's kind of romantic. 
 Those are my top three Sarah Dessen boys from my top three Sarah Dessen reads. (I really need to reread Along for the Ride and Lock and Key, though I seem to recall a really good macking session in the latter.) Sarah Dessen ran my life for a while. I went to a book signing, and she is one of the cutest humans to ever cute, just as you would expect. I read her blog all the time. 
 Then What Happened to Goodbye well... happened. It wasn't bad. In fact, I suspect that a lot of what bothered me with that book can be chalked up to my having too personal a relationship with it. (All the moving.) But I know that other readers cited a sort of missing charm. And I'm afraid that struck again with The Moon and More. 
 Now, after this incredibly long introduction, here's what I actually think of this actual book. (I feel almost like I have to apologize for feeling, for the second time in a row, underwhelmed by a Dessen book. That's how much I love her other books.) 
 I won't make a "what I like" section because A) I'm so inconsistent in how I review things whatever I won't bother this time it's been a while since I finished this one and B) what I liked about TMaM is what I like about every Dessen book. The area felt authentic, the supporting characters felt real. There's a quality to her books that make you feel like you could go to any basic Southern town and meet her characters, go to her shops. 
 TMaM was comfortable. And at first, I was hooked. I blazed through the first hundred pages or so. The backstory was great. Emaline's conflict with her father felt real and wasn't resolved the way I thought it would be, which is fantastic. In fact, most of the "family" issues in this novel were my favorite parts. Again, there were moments that made me as a person uncomfortable because I related overmuch--but those are an individual's complaints. 
 It's just... Look. I don't read Dessen's books just for the main character, just for the family. Her earlier reads were "younger" and less romance-centric; Dreamland was a total departure, and it was great. But ever since This Lullaby, I think that Dessen readers have come to expect a certain... thing... from her works. 
 The Dessen Boy. 
 And The Dessen Boy was exactly where TMaM began to go wrong. 
 Really, you sort of have two boys here. Luke, the longtime boyfriend--handsome, charming, totally generic, totally flawed in a realistic manner. And Theo--artsy, wears girls' jeans, "changes" Emaline's perspective on things. 
 This is when I started to realize that Emaline wasn't doing anything. She had an issue with Luke or Theo? She said nothing. She did nothing. She passive aggressively hated on every try-hard thing Theo did like it was some kind of crime when he couldn't have known better, being an outsider to her world. She never tried to help him learn or give him a shot at becoming "one of them". She just categorized him as an outsider, like every other person of Colby. 
 Which bugged me. Because I have played the role of both the hometown girl and the unintentionally pretentious outsider. And God, Emaline doesn't have to totally "get" Theo. But I felt like she wasn't growing, and he wasn't growing, and their "romance" was taking a really obvious direction throughout the book and... The character development just didn't do it for me. 
 Even when it came to her issues with her father, I felt like Emaline never said her piece. And maybe that's authentic. Yet it got really boring and really repetitive and at the end of the book I was, dare I say it, skimming a bit. Because I knew how this was going to end. 
 Basically: it was fine, but fine isn't good enough when I know that Sarah Dessen can do better. 
 The Cover: I miss her old, less photorealistic covers that focused on hands. This one's cute, if bland. I do like the marshiness, as it reminds me of not only Colby but my home. 3/5

I probably should have written this review right after finishing the book. Instead, I finished Requiem and now I have to backtrack. In fact I put off reading this book for months until the release of Requiem was closer. It came sooner than expected and I am glad because I really enjoyed Pandemonium, it was more exciting than I thought it would be. I wasn't sucked in right away and I wasn't a fan of the Then/Now flashbacks right away. But I'll admit - the ending, wow!, it was awful and great at the same time. 
 It was hard reading about Lena, alone and without Alex. Everything she deals with is so harsh and brutal that her experiences become much more realistic and her pain is reasonable. I don't know how I feel about Raven. I'm in the air about her maybe because I'm biased with this being Lena's story.  I know being an outlaw leader can't be easy but I may have been more hurt and deceived than Lena was when she learns her captivity with Julian was a known and planned setup.  
 Lauren Oliver does have a remarkable writing style in which the harsh realities of Lena's new world become real and vivid imaginings the readers can transform from the likeness of their own backyard. And Julian, it was hard to accept him but as the story continues he goes thorough the same journey Lena did with Alex, where she has to decide if the world and society they live in is actually 'Right' and if the disease of love (deliria) is actually worth fighting for. 
 This book was definitely a thriller. There was action and adventure and more bad guys than I could count. I found the addition of the Scavengers to be well placed. For me they represented a group of people who defy one cause and don't see fit to take up another. Survival of the fittest at its best. Even the people hidden the sewers were unique in their identities and brought a helpful edge to the cause as it turns out there were a lot more people aside from the Invalids and Scavengers alive whom were cast out of society. 
 I'm still very upset with Raven.  I know she had to make a choice, for the good of her people, but I think it goes against the cause to go behind the backs of those who trust you and put them in danger without them knowing the facts.  Also, now that I'm so worked up, I will point out that there was a character error when they are running in the Wilds. Hunter is apparently carrying Blue when he had not yet returned from the hunting party. 
 I am very proud of Lena in this book. She holds nothing back. Her weakness and her strengths are all tested and even when she fails she finds the will to go on.  I found it interesting when she was up on the catwalk above where Julian was going to get 'his procedure,' very similar to Alex watching over her if I remember correctly in Delirium.  
 Overall 
 I really enjoyed Pandemonium, more than I thought I would. Life is not easy for Lena in the Wilds. It would not be easy for anyone who enjoys all the basic luxuries of everyday life. Things we normally take for granted like running water, toilets, silverware... Lena's struggle becomes real and gripping. This book starts off a bit slow but begins to pick up pace and before you know it, you're sucked in. I would recommend it to dystopian fans and readers of book one, Delirium.

I'm sorry it took me this long to find this series. This review will apply to the four books currently published, though I see there is a fifth in the works and I cannot wait to read it. 
 At first it seems like your standard thief fantasy. Interesting politics, skilled main character with a dark wit, compelling secondary characters. But then it takes a twist for the superb. It's hard to review this book without giving away the surprise, but suffice it to say that Eugenides is not what he seems. Not by a long shot. Instead he is a lovable, flawed, tortured but not quite brooding, and ridiculously clever character to compete with Kvothe of The Name of the Wind. But he has even more tricks up his sleeve. 
 The author can make the most shocking surprise seem completely believable. It makes for a thrilling read. The first three books especially blew me away. Each time I was so startled I gasped, and yet I felt silly for not seeing it coming sooner. The dialogue is witty and frequently poignant, making even the most minor character seem real. Each of them have their own motives, schemes and plots in the works. But only Eugenides is able to see them all. At times I was heartbroken for him; he is one of the most abused characters I have ever read. Somehow, though, each time his intellect and wit win out over all obstacles. 
 The fourth book is different in tone because there is a different narrator, but I enjoyed Sophos as well. He is a very different main character, more compassionate and kind, but no less intelligent and no less capable of great things than his thief friend. 
 Throughout the series, the exploration of the religion is fascinating. The gods are characters themselves, and the mythology is as much a part of the story and the characters as the actual events. Eugenides manages to be "chosen" by the gods without the feeling that anything is predestined or beyond human control. It comes together as one of the most believable mythologies I've read in fantasy. 
 It's interesting that this is classified as a Teen book. Technically the characters are very young, but it reads much more like an adult fantasy. I still recommend it for teens, especially those that want a more mature storyline and characters. If you want a complex plot and twists you won't see coming, do not miss this series.

The third scene with him as the point of view character seemed as though it tried to play as a grand reveal of his continued survival. 
 The villains of the story were not my favorite. They were only in a few scenes and always seemed to have an archvillain feel to them. I would have liked to at least seen a deeper motivation for their deeds. 
 That said, the backdrop characters really lived the plot. Though Laural seemed to lack much in the way of common sense, the rest of the characters where lovable and amusing. I especially enjoyed the Huckabee children and their pranks. I wish there would have been more of them.

i was so excited to read this book.... and i can tell the author really tried, but........ it fell really flat, emotionally, plot-wise, character-wise. i appreciate that lo tried to put a unique spin on it, but i remember glancing down at about page 200 or so and thinking "wait, i'm already 2/3 of the way through? but...when is the story going to start?" 
 i think what happened was that the author got too caught up in mapping the plot out that she lost track of the true heart of the story. it feels like she confused herself with her own setup and just... lost direction because she was trying to do too much, and in the end, that confusion is what sucked all the emotion out of the story. the best relationship was between ash and her dead mom because at least there i understood oh, ash is bawling her eyes out. that must mean she misses her mum. but the rest of the time i was just kind of ????? like, is this random servant girl ash's new love interest? is it huntress #1? huntress #2? is it her stepsister? i could NOT tell, because ash interacts with all of them in the same exact way. she was as intriguing as a piece of white bread. like, i didn't even realize that kaisa was supposed to be her boo basically until they confessed/kissed/i don't even remember how that part resolved itself. there was no tension (not even "hey i'm super important and you're a servant and us hanging out is kinda weird" kind of tension), no flirting (does petting each other's horses count?), not even subtle gay subtext-- and trust me when i say i am a master at picking up subtle gay subtext because i live off the stuff. and then there's sidhean and THERE WERE SO MANY POSSIBILITIES FOR CHARACTER EXPLORATION AND ANGSTY DRAMATIC SCENES WITH THAT DUDE AND WITH ASH and i am SAD and i am SADDER that the gay girl romance fell even flatter than the weird & mystical hetero side-fling. 
 i think lo let herself get swept away by the challenge of recreating such a classic fairytale, and i really think it's a shame because i have all the love for lgbt writers and novels. what i will say is that she has the basic world-building skills and story-telling flow down. as someone who loves character-driven novels though, i would love to see her work on fleshing out her characters, juicing up those relationships, and not losing sight of the passion behind the story. i am cheering u on malinda!

 I love these audiobooks with Santino Fontana narrating (who I did not realize is the voice of Hans in Frozen, thanks to my sister for that tidbit! I love this series and reread the whole thing many times as a kid ( and since then....) but always struggled with this one. I think it's the format, written as letters to Gilbert. There are some well crafted characters and stories here but I never really connected with them until I "met" them in the film version. Just not my cup of tea and I was happy to reconnect with the more familiar format in Anne's House of Dreams.

Some reviewers seem to think this book lacks a central plot, and perhaps that's so, but I still enjoyed listening to it. It has a sort of "aftermath" feel, which makes sense in wake of the disastrous events at the end of the 7th book, but there are also some big events in this one. 
 Some things seemed to happen quite suddenly in this book. A major power shift takes place mostly off-stage and kinda comes out of nowhere. Eric's subdued reaction to that, and to hotel explosion at the end of the last book, were also a little surprising but I guess you don't get to live for 1000 years by being foolishly rash... I was also somewhat caught off guard by Sigebert's actions towards the end because his character seemed to change without warning. But then, he did have the rug pulled out from under him in a major way, and perhaps his reaction makes sense in light of that. 
 There were some good little bits about various side characters in this book. For example, the vampire Pam (one of my favorite vampires) starts dating Amelia Broadway, a witch from New Orleans who becomes Sookie's roommate after the 6th book. This didn't surprise me very much at all; they actually seem like they'd work well as a couple. It was fun to read about them scandalizing Merlotte's. In other parts of the book, you can still see the fallout from Hurricane Katrina. Several hurricane refugees find their way to Bon Temps, and one of them takes up residence with Sookie and Amelia. Katrina also plays a part in the trouble facing the werewolf factions. 
 However, the strength of this book really lies in the insights into characters and the way they change. Sookie is realizing that she has true friends, like Sam and Amelia and even Eric, and connecting with them on a level she couldn't back before all this crazy drama started (like in the first book). She had been guarded and lonely for much of her life, but now her character is starting to interact more with the world at large. She's more outspoken. Part of this also has to do with discovering two relatives--one very old and very strange, one very young--and Sookie is starting to discover what roles they might play in her life as well. 
 And there's a feeling of lost innocence that I thought was pervasive in this book. It's appropriate for a post-disaster story, I thought. Sookie is thinking about all the things that have happened and what she's had to do to survive. She's facing up to the parts of her personality that don't live up to her expectations of what a "good person" should be and trying to accept those things anyway. I think her character grows a lot around this point in the series.

A few years ago I was about to start Jude the Obscure, and I was also about to get divorced, and everyone was like nooooo, do not read this book while you're depressed anyway; it is the bummer of all bummers. So I didn't. I read it just now instead. 
 And I'm not sure that advice was crucial. One of the messages of the book is that one shouldn't stay in a marriage that's not the right marriage; in a way, this might have been reassuring, right? 
 One of the other messages is "But society will beat you down no matter what you do, and then everyone dies alone and miserable." But this is Hardy, so you expect that. 
 Hardy was a free thinker, a realist and a radical. Like Dickens, he was concerned with the lives of the poor - rural poor, mostly, as opposed to Dickens' London poor. He was pro-women's rights. He was some weird homebrewed species of agnostic. Sue Bridehead is a fascinating, complicated character: skeptical, rebellious, self-destructive. Jude the Obscure raised such a scandal on publication that Hardy never wrote another novel, which is a shame because he's totally awesome. 
 Hardy has a knack for brilliantly creative scenes. At one point two characters break up, and the whole thing is carried out via notes passed by schoolboys between classrooms. It's fantastic. He's melodramatic and overwrought in a highly entertaining way. 
 And, yes, he's the bummer of all bummers. But he's riveting to read, also; it's the best kind of bummer, and this book is wonderful.

A captivating story with stunning worldbuilding and deep characters. The wizard's apprentice story has been done hundreds of times, but Naomi Novik made it feel fresh and new. 
 The Dragon, who steals young women, is actually a wizard. And he doesn't harm the young women at all. Or so they say. He works to protect the kingdom against the evils of the Wood--so who can complain that he needs a new peasant girl to work for him every ten years? 
 I absolutely loved the character of Agnieska, and how she is a perfect foil for Dragon, but they must learn to work together. There are so many twists and turns in this novel, so much beauty and adventure. I had a hard time putting it down once I got started. In fact, I'm pretty sure I neglected dinner and a number of other tasks. 
 If you're looking for a great, fresh fantasy, with an amazing female heroine, this books for you. 
 Content: It's an adult novel, and has several sexual scenes. 
 Some rather major spoilers: 
 -I liked that when Agnieska went to the city, she defied genre tropes and never learned to integrate into high society or play their games. 
 -I like that love and romance is not the most important thing for Agnieska. She is not going to chase after Dragon--she knows what she wants, and if he won't be part of that, it's his choice. That said, I did like the very end of the book. 
 -The impacts of the dead number of people are devastating. In some ways she doesn't completely deal with that at the end--but perhaps it is impossible to really deal with it.

Check out pageofnoreturn.wordpress.com for more reviews. This review was completed after reading 77 pages of Slaughterhouse-Five. 
 The Reason for the Reaping: As with any classic novel, it's embarrassing that that I haven't read it yet. The war story of all war stories, the time for Slaughterhouse-Five--and always will be--now. 
 As I Lay Summarizing: A man named Billy Pilgrim is living in two worlds: his life as an optometrist, and his life as a soldier during WWII. What is past and what is present is mind-bendingly unclear. So it goes (Yes, that is from this book). 
 The Line That Killed Me: "And I asked myself about the present: how wide it was, how deep it was, and how much of it was mine to keep" (18). Death by deep existential awe. 
 Best Character: Billy Pilgrim 
 Why [As] You Like It: Vonnegut is truly a herald of the American war story. Any story with guns and wartime misery clearly has influence from this novel. Vonnegut = King. Start with stark, moody, and searing prose; add existential disillusion; and spread over time and space. Indeed, this is the war story of all war stories. 
 Why I'm Gone, Girl: Vonnegut is very clearly tapping into the consciousness of wartime and post-war America. As such, white male characters dominate the story, and the experiences of women and people of color are omitted and on some level dismissed. I'm calling you out, Kurt; this is 2017. 
 Last Line, Last Chance: "...would be another click." 
 Will I turn the page, or toss it into Mount Doom? Vonnegut writes with sensitivity and with purpose. This book put him on the map for a reason. The page has been turned. So it goes.

I really enjoyed this sequel. I'd probably rate it 4.5 stars if I was able. The author comes up with really interesting school settings. Shoreline was nothing like Sword and Cross, but I loved the set up. I said it before, but I think Lauren Kate is a great writer and she can create such memorable images/settings. 
 I'm so glad that Daniel didn't stick by the rules of the truce completely and still snuck around the campus to visit Luce every couple of nights. I was really worried in the beginning that Daniel would be completely absent for the vast majority of the book (which, needless to say, would have sucked). They had some really sweet, clandestine meetings, though there was a lot of fighting too. But I think their arguments were important for them to have and necessary in the growth of their relationship. With a love as complicated and forbidden as theirs is, there needs to be some not-so-perfect moments between them. 
 And I am happy to report that I still like Luce (it's been a pattern for me lately to have the heroines in paranormal series to suddenly become awful and frustrating to read about-not the case with this series). She is an awesome, independent girl, which is rare to see in a paranormal romance. She knows that Daniel is her true love, but she also knows that she shouldn't make him her whole world and follow him blindly. She has questions about her past and she is concerned about her future and she'll fight hard to get all the answers she needs. 
 I'm really looking forward to the third book, which I hear is set up to be a prequel to Fallen. I only hope that it ties up the cliff hanger at the end. I mean, Luce did travel inside the Announcer to find out more about her past lives, so it makes sense that the author would include her and Daniel's present journeys while she tells about their past too.  Can't wait! It'll be so great to read all about Daniel and Luce's past lives.

I have read the covenant series by Jennifer L. Armentrout {& loved it}, but when I heard that she had a series about aliens, I was "ehhh" about it. I really hate to start something and not finish, but I hate reading books that don't pull me in, so I decided to read this novella first.... just to get a taste of series and to determine if I wanted to keep going. 
 & O-M-G! I am so happy that I did!! Who knew that aliens could be so entertaining?? From the moment I started reading, I was hooked. I finished the three books {so far} in the series in two days. I could not stop reading. 
 I definitely did not expect to read an alien series that was so mesmerizing. If you have any doubts about reading this series, please just it a shot. It will be worth it.

What, that's it??? I need book 2 now!!!!! 
 Okay, so since I've literally just finished this book about a minute ago, I need to get some stuff off my chest - and this is the reason Roar did not get a full 5 stars from me. 
 I love this story. Seriously freaking love it - it's intriguing, creative, and wholly original. I've never read a story about storms having souls. It's awesome! 
 Unfortunately, there was all this build up (which I love and it really kept my attention) but it never really went anywhere. Well, that's not exactly true. We got the build up, but we never got the climax. There are so many cliffhangers, which I imagine will be the focus of book 2, but we weren't left with anything for book 1. So much is put into motion, but it's not seen through. And I feel kind of let down and that this is a bit unfair. I've just read 378 pages of great character development, world building, and plot progression, but it nothing really gets resolved. I get that Carmack wants to leave more stuff for the sequel, but as a reader, I'm a bit upset. It kinda feels like I've been teased with all this awesome stuff that's going to happen, but whoops, haha, gotta wait at least a year for book 2. Not cool. More should have been resolved in this installment of the series. Who is this Stormlord? When will the hunter crew find out Roar's real identity? What is she going to do about Cassius and Pavan? What's going on with Nova? All that really happened in this story is that we learn Roar's abilities. Which is cool and unexpected, but after reading so much and getting so invested, I need more than just that.  
 Anyways, now that I've gotten that out of the way, onto the character's! I love all of them and the diversity of them. I love getting to see Rora develop into a more confident person, I loved to get to read about Cassius - he's actually a bit of a hard read, does he care for Aurora at all, or is it just a farce? Cause it seems to lean more to the former, when we're supposed to think the latter. 
 Locke had me swinging all kind of ways, some times I was rooting for him, other times I wanted him to get off of Roar's back - she can handle herself, she is not a damsel in distress! But he really only has the best of intentions for her, so I can't fault him for trying to protect her. I just wish he would realize she can protect herself. 
 Duke and Jinx are two of my faves, and I really like Ransom and Bait too. Sly got on my nerves, but she's has an important role to the story, one that may be overlooked, but there needs to be doubt added in somehow. 
 Mostly, I want to know more about Nova. We're left hanging with her, and I'm very curious about her story. 
 The magic and fantasy of this novel is outstanding and a whole lotta fun. Powerful, sentient (?) storms, storm hunters, stormlings, and battles of the heart - literally. Lots of action. I am very intrigued by the powers displayed in this novel, and want to know lots more. 
 Also, I love the snippets of information before each chapter. I always looked forward to what line of poetry or sentences from tales that we would get. These pages engaged me even more. 
 Action, romance, deceit, power, strength, friendships, I could keep going. This novel has them all. Carmack has beautiful descriptions and lovely sentences throughout the novel, which only enhances the feeling of being connected to the story like Roar is with the storms!  A really enchanting writing style. 
 Cora Carmack, you have achieved your dream of creating a YA fantasy novel, one that is intense, fantastical, kickass, and just plain amazing. Despite my earlier notes of basically being left high and dry, I loved every second of this book. It sucked me in and refused to let me go until this very last word. To put it simply, I was mesmerized.

3.5 stars. Her Fearful Symmetry is an inventive, atmospheric ghost story that left me with mixed feelings. I thought the story was compelling, but I wish there had been more explanation of certain elements. It would be hard to follow up a book as incredible as The Time Traveler's Wife, but I think Niffenegger has done a fine job with this novel.

I loved the setting, enjoyed the love story, enjoyed the mystery. The story was just a little too long. Not that I have anything against long books, but if a book is going to be long, it should be entertaining throughout. I would have enjoyed this book better with a good 100-150 pages cut from it.

In 480 B.C., an invading Persian army, two-million strong, came to the mountain pass of Thermopylae in eastern Greece. Led by King Xerxes, they were met by the finest three hundred Spartan warriors where the rocky confines were so narrow that the Persian multitudes and their cavalry would be at least partially neutralized. Here, the Greek loyalists hoped, the elite force could hold off, at least for a short while, the invading millions. 
 The well-known story of the 300 Spartans lies in the base of this book, but it is much more than that. 
 It is told from the PoV of a PoW, a young man called Xeones, who served under a Spartan officer and fought in the battle of the Hot Gates, against millions of assembled nations of the Persian Empire under Xerxes. 
 As the only living survivor, he tells his story to a Persian scribe, who writes it down for the king, not only the battle itself, but his whole life, his desire to serve Sparta, the lessons he learned and the people he met, all who has made such a lasting impression on him, who became his friends and brothers-in-arms. 
 If this isn't the ultimate book about the famous 300, it should be. 
 Written sometimes with almost military precision, it's a literary masterpiece, for all genders and ages. 
 The plot, sometimes vast, sometimes intimate, always flowing, jumping back in time when necessary, to complete the picture of Sparta and its people. 
 Though at times the military scenes can read too modern, unsurprising as the author himself a former soldier, I can only quote one of my favourite TV characters Geoffrey Tennant as a justification :"War is war, soldiers are soldiers, ambition is ambition". 
 Even more than the plot, I loved the characters, each an individual, with stories of their own. And isn't it funny that the best male characters I ever read about were written by women and the best female ones were written by men?

First of all, WOW. I don't know what I was expecting from The Bone Season, but it was not that. The Bone Season follows Paige Mahoney, who is from an Irish family that migrated to London to find a safe haven and a place to live. In London Paige finds herself introduced to Jaxon Hall, the mime-lord in I-4. There she finds a family of people like herself, but she still isn't safe from Scion, and soon finds herself in Oxford, now known as Scheol I, the city overtaken by a humanoid race called the Rephaim who arrived through the aether 200 years ago. Paige is now XX-59-40, and is taken in by the blood-consort, who may not be as he first appears. 
 I loved everything about this book, in all honesty. Samantha Shannon's writing is fantastic. She built a great alternate universe/dystopian-esque world. I loved the way she interweaved Paige's memories with Warden's abilities, and so we're actually experiencing it as Paige is reliving it rather than being thrown back and forth in time. Everything is relevant. The characters were really well developed, I enjoyed seeing Warden coming into his own rather than just being the enemy or someone Paige hated. I also liked seeing the way the different people either fell into the roles the Rephaim had demanded them to take and how others fought against it, how some seemed to be falling into roles to turn around and do something rebellious. 
 The world in TBS is really interesting. I'm intrigued about the politics of it all and I can't wait to see more of Scion on The Mime Order (because I'm guessing that's where they'll be for most of the novel) after they spent most of this one in Sheol I. 
 I really liked that it was clear that the Rephaim were a humanoid race, rather than being depicted as aliens. At first I was kind of concerned that there was going to be a love story between an alien and a human and I'm just not about that life. It's one trope that I just can't get into. So I was glad they were more like humans. I'm intrigued about the whole 'we are death' thing, like, are the Rephaim some kind of spirit? Or ghost or something? The Emim seem more like ghosts but I guess they're both from the aether, same as spirits, so I'm placing them all together in my mind.  
 I'd just like to take a moment for the fact that this is set in England and it uses some English slang that I really loved! The slang was great, and the world was easy for me to picture having already been to the places Paige was in. It'd be interesting to compare maps. 
 But yeah, I absolutely loved this book. It's one of the best books I've read so far this year. I can't wait to read The Mime Order. I'm not sure what I'm going to do when I have to wait for book three!

5/5 
 I enjoyed Stalking Darkness even more than Luck in the Shadows, which I gave 5/5 stars, as well, so I think it's pretty evident that I loved it. 
 If I have to highlight flaws, I'd say some of the technical incongruities that I mentioned in my review of Luck in the Shadows remain the same. Also, some of the passages in Beka's point of view dragged on a bit, mostly because I wanted to find out what was happening with Alec and Seregil, but I still adored the book. These were all small flaws, and, well... 
 OH MY GOD, IT PUT ME THROUGH AN EMOTIONAL RINGER. I guess one thing I'm worried about is, after the events of Stalking Darkness, what more CAN happen? It had a lot of fun moments, sure, such as the often humorous development of Seregil and Alec's relationship (boys, come on, you're both sleeping with prostitutes who look like each other! What do you think that means?), but the characters went through so much agony. I was shocked by how much the deaths of characters like Cilla and even Tym affected me; don't even get me started on Nysander. When I read what happened to him, I literally shouted aloud, "But Dumbledore doesn't die yet! We're only on book two!" 
 Poor Alec was physically, psychologically, verbally and sexually tortured throughout SD. Even the scene with Ylinestra deeply disturbed me, because his consent was manipulated, but when it was implied that Cilla was raped before she died, I teared up. The result of Irtuk Beshar's magic on Thero, sapping his will from him, was horrifying, too. Even a lot of the death's in Beka's sequences, such as that of one twin brother, were written powerfully, despite my hardly knowing those characters. There was a lot of gruesomeness overall, and it really shook me up the way only a strongly written book about characters I'm attached to can. Seregil's depression at the end was warranted and heart-breaking. I'm glad Alec and the Cavishes helped him at least start to overcome it. 
 I'm an emotional wreck right now, but I'm going to begin Traitor's Moon soon. Thank you, Stalking Darkness, for being my light while I was reading Divergent, which I abhorred.

Absolutely fabulous! 
 I fell in love with this book from the very beginning and it's not difficult to figure out why. Not only is the cover art for this debut novel breathtaking, but the story itself is intriguing and wonderfully researched. 
 Calla Tor is an alpha for the Nightshade pack, Guardians, she leads her young pack and is the perfect warrior for the Keepers they are sworn to fight for. Everything is planned and provided for them, including who they'll mate with, and when Calla unthinkingly saves a human from a bear attack, she sets things in motion that were probably better left unknown. 
 With her union to Ren, the alpha for the young Bane pack, coming up soon, she can't afford to have any distractions. And that's what Shay Doran is, the human that she saved. And to her disappointment (and pleasure) he ends up being the one the Keepers ask Calla to protect from their enemies the Searchers. 
 This is a story of duty and responsibility, of following your heart and falling in love, of secrets and betrayal. Andrea Cremer does an absolutely amazing job of describing the world she's created; everything from the shifts between wolf and human, the hierarchy of Keepers, Searchers, and Guardians, even the contrast between Calla's feelings toward Ren and Shay. There's so much more going on then Calla or the other guardians know, and Andrea Cremer goes into just enough detail to leave you wanting to know more. 
 I was so disappointed when I got to the last page and realized that I had reached the end of of this amazing book and found myself wishing that Wolfsbane (Book 2) was already out. I can't say enough good things about this book, and I don't want to give anything away, but if you're looking for a unique tale about magic and wolves then this would be it.

 Then one day, Jase Garrett climbs the terrace and this is where their relationship begins. There is so much more to this story and I am being very vague to avoid spoilers, but seriously read this book people! Don't let their young age fool you (I don't always like YA books), this is truly a beautiful story and worth every second!

{Notes} 
 * WARNING: this contains spoilers. It's hard to talk about what's wrong with this book without them, so be careful. Also, obvious potential for spoilers on books 1 and 2. 
 * I'm having a really hard time deciding what to rate this. This was just so, so...disappointing. It hurts to rate it this low, considering Delirium was probably one of my favorite reads of the year. But it is what it is. 
 * The writing is still beautiful. It's lyrical and poetic and gives me tingles in all the right ways. Unfortunately, it's about the only thing I felt good about in the end. 
 * Maybe this needed to be a series instead of a trilogy? Maybe four books instead of three? Nothing happens for what feels like forever, then bam! It's all over. Maybe one book to sort out Lena's feelings about the boys and her mom and family. Maybe another to fight the war? I don't know. 
 * Lena was just...annoying. I loved her in Delirium. I loved her character progression in Pandemonium. In Requiem, she turns into a whiny little brat that doesn't know which toy she likes better. Yes, she's still brave, and she's still strong when it comes to fighting, but she acts so stupid in every other scene, you almost forget about how awesome she can be. 
 * Alex and Julian. Why? I mean, really. We haven't seen the love triangle enough? Honestly, I never connected with Alex. I saw him as an ends to a mean: Lena discovering herself and how to love. Julian was so well-developed in Pandemonium. Their relationship felt real and grounded. Hopeful. Just what like learning to love again after heartbreak is supposed to be. In Requieum, he's reduced to a background character that Lena occasionally shares a tent with when she's not moping about Alex. And fine, ya know, if she's supposed to end up with Alex, at least give me a single reason to support it. Alex acts like an ass the entire book, then runs away because he "obviously" loves her more and wants her to be happy. Really? Really?! 
 * Alex and Lena's reunion in the end is lame. Especially since she's still apparently eying Julian's strong and sweaty musculature. Make up your damn mind, girl! 
 * I love finally meeting Lena's mother. I wish we'd gotten more from her. More interaction, more emotion. It's been such a huge part of Lena's quest, and it's reduced to pretty much the last fourth of the book. 
 * Coral was pretty awesome. Some serious missed opportunities there, I think. 
 * I actually enjoyed Hana's side of the story. It broke up the monotony of Lena's boy debates. She was perfectly stoic, just like a cured person is supposed to be, but I loved seeing more and more of the cracks show. The whole storyline with Fred was deliciously sinister. It really could have gone somewhere dark if it had been played out fully. The allusions to Bluebeard, his first wife...gah! It just pains me that all these threads are fluttering in the wind. 
 * NO RESOLUTION. None. For not a single character. I get that it's some big statement about not knowing what's coming is part of being human, blah, blah, blah. I got it two books ago. Just chopping off the end of the story before any plot thread resolves is just silly. We don't officially know who Lena chooses. We don't know where the rest of her family is. We don't know about any of the secondary characters from the Wilds: is Raven really dead, where is Tack, etc.? We don't know if the bomb got Fred and what Hana's going to do next. We don't even know if they win the effing fight! Just one big pile of disappointment when I realized there wasn't any left. It needed an epilogue or something. 
 * It really just felt like a whole lotta nothing happened. I'd expect this from a middle book of a trilogy, not the grand finale. 
 * Not to mention, I found a couple of what I assume to be editing errors (hardcover, first edition). Repeated words that didn't make sense. Not cool for publishing a novel of this category. 
 * I just, yeah...I don't know what else to say. I feel let down. Honestly, read the first two books and quit. It's not worth it. You don't get anymore resolution than the cliffhanger ending of book two. This could have been infinitely better, and was poorly handled. While Delirium may be one of my unrivaled favorites, this is far from it. *sadface* 
 ******* 
 A brief note on 'Alex'... 
 I bought the first edition hardcover, so I got the bonus 'Alex' short story in the back. I have to say, it was kind of disappointing as well. It was a huge shock to go from such anger and disappointment over the ending of the series to trying to remember the feelings from the first book, when Alex and Lena were in love. 
 While I liked seeing the insight from his point of view, overall, I found it to be bland and boring. He goes through some really dark stuff that could have been explored, but instead, we basically get a really, really quick recap of what Alex does from Delirium to Pandemonium. It felt disjointed and like nothing really belonged together. I wish the author had just picked one point in his life and went with it, not hop-skipping all over the place. 
 Overall, I didn't feel like it really gave me any insight into Alex's head.
A cute world, with lots going on, but don't feel like I'm going to want to see what happens next.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This is actually one of the first book I've read not only recommended to me by someone, but bought for me. I got it for my birthday back in November with the explicit instructions to "read it because it will change [my] life." I have been harassed ever since to read it. 
 Now, was it life changing? Not quite, but it was an amazing book. It was romantic and heartbreaking all at once. It centers around Juliet and her discovery of a literary society and the German occupation of the channel islands of Britain. 
 The heart-wrenching part of this book is hearing everyone's stories; stories that, in all likelihood, are true. The thing about WWII books is that, even the fictional ones, the stories have to come from some where. So even though Guernsey and Juliet and Amelia and Elizabeth and Dawsey and everyone else we interact with may be made up... I would bet a large sum of money that the stories that they pass back and forth are as real as the paper they're written on. And that's the part that kills you because some of them are so tragic, so heart breaking, you can barely contain your grief. 
 I really loved seeing everyone's introductions to books. Honestly, it was my favorite part. I've had the pleasure of watching a few people who had no love for literature find that ONE BOOK that completely changed their minds. Reading about the literary society and how books not only changed their lives but saved their lives, well, it's this magical moment. To see that, you really feel privileged that you get to see that moment in a person's life. 
 While I understand that in a book about a literary society there are going to be a inundated amount of references to other authors, the written resemblances to their works really put me off. Charles Lamb and how closely his life resembled Jane Eyre's, not to mentions Dawsey's own touch of madness in his life. And then there's the fact that the entire novel read a little like a Jane Austen novel, except for the part where it's written in letters so we get a little bit of LeClos. It would have been nice to seen the writers bring out their own style while referencing other authors as opposed to the incredible resemblance they made to the literary geniuses. And since they were so often referencing those geniuses, it was really easy to make the liaisons. 
 I love the relationships that developed in this book, though the predictability got to me. The second Dawsey showed up I knew he'd end up with Juliet. I knew Sydney would always be a brotherly figure to Juliet (though, I admit, I didn't see the homosexual aspect.) I knew Mark would be a colossal jerk and I knew that Elizabeth, wonderful Elizabeth, would never return. As wonderful as the story was, I just wish I didn't know what was going to happen before it, you know... happened. And I mean, we're not talking a few pages or a chapter before. I mean I knew EONS before it happened that it was going to happen. 
 Overall, I enjoyed the book. It was good and heartwarming and a great post-war read. It let's you see the tragedy that was WWII but still let you believe in the hope of the post-war. I recommend picking it up.

On the plus side, this is a much more romantic (and happy) take on The Return of Martin Guerre and Summersby. After being widowed and reduced to poverty by tacky, greedy relatives, Larissa (Lara)'s husband Hunter, Lord Hawksworth miraculously returns from the dead. Years before, Hunter had set sail for India and was presumed dead in a shipwreck. 
 Lara had a very unhappy marriage and the prospect of welcoming Hunter back throws her into turmoil. On the one hand, he was a drunken, womanizing lout. Then again, his return means her own return to what was once her rightful place in society. To complicate matters, this Hunter seems to have turned over a new leaf. Not only has he abandoned his dissolute old ways, but he actually seems interested in Lara as a human being. 
 At times, this book is deliciously romantic. Hunter is a fantastic hero, and I quite enjoyed what we learned of him. He's a caring person and obviously devoted to Lara, but most definitely not a pushover. I found Lara much more difficult to like. This book was written in the late 90s, and Lara is one of the early prototypes of The Bland Saintly Heroine. Her life pretty much revolves around her good works in the community and yes, she does take in an orphan over the course of this story. Being charitable doesn't make one an annoying heroine, but having not much by way of identity outside of one's charitable works certainly does. 
 Lara's life pretty much seems to consist of obsessing over her works and alternately enticing Hunter and pushing him away. I could understand her reluctance to jump wholeheartedly into a relationship with her husband, given their history, but the ambivalence went on for sooo long. At times in the story, some of the less sympathetic characters make cracks about Lara's perceived lack of intelligence and I reluctantly found myself agreeing with the villains on that point at times. 
 In addition to the tensions of reunion, the story gets an extra jolt of tension as the question of whether Hunter is who he says he is gets introduced. I won't spoil the story by talking about how that shakes out, but I will say that I did end up liking the resolution of this book even if Lara did wear on my nerves pretty severely at times.

The only thing stopping me from giving this book five stars is that I possess strong dislike for Stan and Charmaine. Stan is arguably frustrating, because he is so much of a negative individual, the imaginary cheating, the stalking and obsession of imaginary Jasmine, and his sexual thoughts about women he meets. And he was completely happy to let his wife undergo an operation which would make her at his beck and call, effectively removing her free will. 
 Charmaine, on the other hand, I find far more frightening. The way she justifies her actions, particularly her cheating on Stan, speaks volumes on the state of her mind. Not to mention her insistence that love be something uncontrollable and completely devoid of choice. Upon discovering that she never underwent the operation removing her free will, her immediate thoughts were that it couldn't be possible to be contentedly happy and love her husband without such operation - and she immediately imagined a life with someone else. Her mind welcomes chaos and the lack of culpability that goes along with it. "Can't help myself" would be the argument she would pose - which seems as if she refuses to take any responsibilities for her actions.  
 Such an interesting read, though. Margaret Atwood always manages to make me think hard about the idea of free will, and what some people would do to curb it. And sometimes, what we ourselves would do to curb it just so we could justify our actions as uncontrollable.

 If you think you're about to read an archaeological treatise on the discovery of a truly 'lost city' - a word true archaeologists hate - then fuhgeddaboudit. (Did I spell that right, all you Soprano-lovers out there?) This is a story about a discovery by a writer who writes adventure-mystery-suspense novels, sometimes with a writing partner. His adventure-mystery-suspense books are great! Did I say great? They are among my most favorite books, and I don't give a hoot if anyone criticizes my grammar, spelling or syntax. :D 
 So the book is written from a different sort of perspective than one might expect. This is NOT Erik Larson - whose books I also love - or a renowned, 60-ish historian/anthropologist/archaeologist. This book is written from the POV of a guy who knows words and knows suspense, but is actually just a regular guy so he writes about regular stuff. About how astounded he is to be on this project. About the people working around him. About the jungle, its animals - its SNAKES! - and how he spent most of his time in the Honduran jungle soaking wet, constantly being bitten by something. 
 I loved this point of view. It's one I don't often see in books which are about something which really happened. Plus I have always loved 'lost cities' and as a child had a book with a green cover with that name on it exactly: LOST CITIES. I mean, political scientific correctness aside - and I've got a degree in Biology, btw - how many kids grew up and wanted to be archaeologists, historians or anthropologists just because of that book, or books like it? 
 So what's it about? About the discovery of a city in the jungles of Honduras, an area where even the looters and local drug smugglers haven't gone. The city is HUGE, but hidden by centuries of forestation. There are pyramids and plazas, a court for playing handball. The city has some elements which are 'Maya-like,' but many which are not. It appears to have been deserted centuries ago for reasons unknown, though there are a lot of hypotheses about that. (Archaeologists love to speculate on all this stuff, and argue, both among themselves and with people like Preston and the others who made this find. The arguing can get rather petty at times, IMO.) One of the first finds uncovered is a cache of objects - beautifully carved jaguars, vultures and other animals. 
 It's all of this which makes the book so fascinating. The jungle, the bugs, the people, the weather (mostly rainy), the animals, the nearly impassable terrain. It's also loaded with scientific details, including a fascinating explanation of 'lidar' which I followed completely, as well as information on the culture, environment, biology and history of the area in which the 'lost city' was found. 
 This book was great and though it ended on a creepy note - a discussion of leishmaniasis, a parasitic disease which Preston and several of his co-explorers contracted, and which some of them are still struggling with years later - this book was the one I carried around the house with me. When I had two minutes here, ten there, half an hour or so, I read this book. I devoured this book. One of my family members said, is that book attached to you, or what? :D 
 Of course I'd read almost anything Mr. Preston writes, but that's not the point. It's simply a wonderful book. 
 Five stars

I absolutely love Goodreads. I love the infinite lists and recommendations and my never-ending to read list. However, there is one thing I miss about life before Goodreads and that's the joy of discovering books in a bookshop simply by looking at a cover and reading the synopsis, no reviews, no ratings. Nowadays, almost all the books I read are based on what I've researched and decided on before even leaving the house. I have found some of my absolute favourite books this way, however, it's taken some of the joy out of going to a bookshop. 
 So this time, I took a risk and picked this up from my local bookshop without ever having heard of it. I didn't recognize the writer, I hadn't seen it in any list and I didn't quickly check the rating with my phone. The cover was beautiful though, the first page was interesting and the synopsis told me it was a portal fantasy. It made me realise how truly long it had been since I read a portal fantasy. It's true that they've fallen out of fashion. Right now serious fantasy is all about hard magic and intricate world building in another universe with no connection to ours and I love it. However, there is something nostalgic about a simple good old portal fantasy where you get everything explained to you because the main character needs the information and you always have pop culture references because the MC just can't stop themselves from making wierd comments and being met by confused stares of other characters. Portal fantasy may be old fashioned, but it's easy and comfortable and fun. 
 So I picked this up, I started reading and then I regretted my choice within the first ten pages. The writing seemed so unbelievably clumsy. The narrative voice was strange, the shifts between POVs was clumsy and there was an info dump every few pages. As soon as we entered the new world, it was like the author was standing there with a huge red sign saying "Here are a bunch of weird sounding words to cover up the fact that there isn't really that much world building!" 
 The thing with finding books on Goodreads is that while there are still a lot of times where I don't like a book or don't see what the hype was about, those are generally cases of personal opinion. Books that get famous on Goodreads usually at least have good writing and meet the basics of everything. In the first few chapters, it seemed to me that I should just stick with that method from now and save myself all the trouble of reading badly written books with nice covers. 
 Then, however, something magical happened.  The main character got her fingers chopped off! Not seriously, though that was cool.  The book started improving rapidly. After the author stepped away from bombarding me with information I could actually see that there was some decent world building beneath all the thermology. The magic may not have been the structured, limited hard magic of new fantasy but it wasn't just some convenient problem solver either. In fact, it didn't play that big of a part in the book, instead, it focused on the characters and through them, it tackled so many big issues so boldly. Race, gender, sexuality and disability were all freely discussed, yet it didn't feel overwhelming or preachy, just a natural part of the characters' lives. 
 Speaking of characters, they're one of the strongest points of this book. They're interesting, complicated people who actually have bad shit happen to them. They don't get out of every situation unscathed, in fact, they don't get out of any situation without sacrificing something. That's the most modern aspect of the book, that our heroes are actually human and aren't in possession of some sort of supernatural luck which lets them just walk in and out of dangerous situation after dangerous situation without a hair out of place. 
 Saffron reacts to this new world in a way that actually seems real. She doesn't turn into some superhero warrior badass in a day. They give her an axe and she swings it like a Tennis racket. She feels confused and overwhelmed, but also excited because she is in a FREAKING new world. She worries about what's happening back home. She gets hurt and her actions in this world aren't a separate part of her life but they have real and lasting consenquences. She isn't perfect, she worries about her a scar affects her looks even though she knows it's vain and she acknowledges it. She notices when she is acting unconsciously racist and stops herself. She is capable and smart and strong. A heroine worth reading about. 
 There are many other points I wanted to go through, but in the end what really matters is that it's different. It's not mainstream fantasy, it's not just another portal fantasy either. It's something worth taking a chance on, even though that's the last thing I thought I would say when I first started reading it.

This was a lovely, well-written book about 2 young people growing up during World War II. Marie Laure is a french girl that loses her sight at a very young age. He is very smart and interested in learning and it is these traits that will get him picked out from the other children to train to be a Nazi. 
 This book had really wonderful characters. Marie Laure is sweet and curious and I loved her story and seeing things from her perspective. Just as interesting though is Werner's story as we get to see how this nice young man gets to be part of the Nazi army. I thought the author did a fantastic job letting us get to know these characters and helping us to understand the choices that they made. 
 The story itself is not always very fast paced as a lot of it is simply seeing how these two live their lives day to day but this worked really well as I wanted to learn more about these characters and how their lives worked. The writing is excellent and I was easily able to pictures these characters and the lives they live. 
 Overall, this was an excellent book and I would highly recommend it to someone looking for a historical fiction book based on this time period. There are definitely sad moments to the book but nothing too graphic so it would be an excellent book for even young teens to read. This is the first book that I have read by this author but I will definitely be checking out other books by him.
